name: Hunnic Empire (Attila)
summary: Nomadic Huns crossed the Volga around 370, subdued the Alans and Goths and by the 420s were based on the Great Hungarian Plain, extorting tribute from both halves of the Roman Empire. Under Attila (sole ruler from c. 445) they ravaged the Balkans, Gaul and Italy, but after his death in 453 the subject peoples revolted at the Nedao and the empire fell apart; his son Dengizich was killed in 469.

events.text: c. 370: Huns reach the Volga and conquer the Alans and Goths
events.detail: The Huns were nomadic horse archers who first appear in Roman sources living east of the Volga river, on the steppe north of the Caspian Sea. Around 370 they crossed the Volga and fell on the Alans, a fellow steppe people, and then on the Gothic kingdoms of what is now Ukraine: first the Greuthungi (eastern Goths), then most of the Thervingi (western Goths). Many of the defeated were absorbed into the Huns' following. The rest fled west. This sudden move set off a chain of migrations that pushed peoples toward the Roman frontier, and it explains why the Huns first appear on the map north of the Black Sea.

events.text: Gothic refugees fleeing the Huns seek shelter on the Lower Danube
events.detail: In the summer of 376 a huge crowd of Goths, driven from their lands by the Huns, gathered on the north bank of the Danube, the Roman border. They were two groups, the Thervingi under Fritigern and Alavivus and the Greuthungi under Alatheus and Saphrax, and they asked the eastern emperor Valens for permission to settle inside the empire, and he let the Thervingi cross. Corrupt Roman officials mistreated the starving refugees, who rebelled. In 378 the Goths destroyed the Roman army and killed Valens at Adrianople. Without crossing the river themselves, the Huns had broken Rome's Danube frontier.

events.text: First large-scale Hun attack on the Eastern Roman Empire
events.detail: By the 390s most Huns were probably living around the Volga and Don rivers. In 395, the year the Roman Empire was finally split between the sons of Theodosius I, they launched their first large-scale attack on the eastern half. Riding through the Caucasus passes, they overran Armenia, pillaged Cappadocia, entered parts of Syria and threatened Antioch, while others raided Thrace. The campaign showed how far and fast Hun horsemen could strike. It was a raid for loot and captives, not a conquest, so it added no lasting territory, but it made the Huns a feared name in the eastern provinces.

events.text: Uldin crosses the Danube and pillages Thrace
events.detail: Uldin is the first Hun leader named in contemporary sources. By about 400 his followers were living north of the lower Danube. At first he was useful to Rome, killing the rebel Gothic general Gainas and helping defend Italy against the Goth Radagaisus, but in 408, knowing that eastern troops had been moved to the Persian frontier, he crossed the Danube, took the fort of Castra Martis and pillaged Thrace. The eastern Romans could not meet his price for peace, so they bribed his subordinates instead, and many of his men deserted. Uldin fled back across the Danube and disappears from history.

events.text: Aetius cedes Pannonia to the Huns
events.detail: By the 420s the Huns had moved their centre to the Great Hungarian Plain, where the open grassland suited their herds. Under King Rugila they worked closely with the western Roman general Flavius Aetius, who had lived among them as a hostage and later used Hun troops against his rivals and against the Goths in Gaul. In return, parts of the Roman province of Pannonia, west and south of the Danube, were ceded to the Huns, probably in 433, though the exact date and extent are disputed. The cession gave the Huns a secure home base astride the Danube, the heart of their empire on the map.

events.text: Attila and Bleda impose the Treaty of Margus on Eastern Rome
events.detail: Rugila died around 434, and his nephews Attila and Bleda took joint power. The next year (435, according to the Attila article) they met envoys of the eastern emperor Theodosius II at Margus, near modern Požarevac in Serbia, all seated on horseback in the Hun manner. The treaty doubled Rome's yearly tribute from 350 to 700 pounds of gold. It also opened markets to the Huns, forbade Rome to ally with the Huns' enemies and required it to return Hun fugitives. Margus showed the new rulers' method: they would use threats of war to drain gold from Constantinople rather than conquer land.

events.text: Attila and Bleda invade the Balkans, sacking Margus and Viminacium
events.detail: In 440 the Huns accused the Romans of breaking the Treaty of Margus and attacked a market town on the Danube. The next year, with the eastern army away fighting in Sicily and Armenia, Attila and Bleda crossed the river in force. At Margus the local bishop, whom they had demanded be handed over, secretly opened the city to them. They sacked Margus and Viminacium, then took Singidunum (Belgrade) and Sirmium; using battering rams and siege towers for the first time, they also stormed Ratiara and Naissus (Niš). The northern Balkans now lay open to Hun armies.

events.text: Peace of Anatolius: Theodosius II pays heavier tribute
events.detail: After a further campaign in 443 the Huns defeated a Roman army outside Constantinople, but they could not break the city's double land walls. Theodosius II, with no army left to resist, sent the general Anatolius to make peace. The terms were far harsher than at Margus. Rome paid a lump sum of 6,000 Roman pounds of gold, and the yearly tribute was tripled to 2,100 pounds. The treaty took no land, but it made the Eastern Roman Empire a tributary of the Huns and paid for the warriors and gifts that held Attila's empire together.

events.text: Bleda dies; Attila becomes sole ruler
events.detail: After the Huns pulled back from the Balkans, Attila's older brother Bleda died, probably around 445. How he died is unknown. The chronicler Jordanes suggests that Attila had him murdered, perhaps on a hunting trip, and a later Hungarian legend claims Attila killed him and threw his body into the Danube. Whatever the truth, Attila was now sole ruler of a vast and loose empire of Huns, Ostrogoths, Gepids, Alans and other subject peoples, stretching from the steppe toward the Rhine. All decisions on war and tribute now rested with one man.

events.text: Attila invades the Balkans and Thrace again
events.detail: In 447 Attila rode south again into the Eastern Roman Empire through Moesia. A Roman army under the Gothic general Arnegisclus met him at the Utus river and was defeated, though it inflicted heavy losses. With no field army left, the Huns rampaged through the Balkans as far south as Thermopylae in Greece. Constantinople survived because the prefect Constantinus quickly rebuilt walls damaged by a recent earthquake. The Romans had to pay again, and a strip of land south of the Danube was reportedly emptied as a buffer, bringing the Hun frontier deep into the Balkans.

events.text: Attila invades Gaul; checked at the Catalaunian Plains
events.detail: In 450 Honoria, sister of the western emperor Valentinian III, sent Attila a plea for help and her ring to escape a forced marriage. Attila treated this as a marriage proposal and demanded half the western empire as her dowry. In 451 he crossed the Rhine, took Metz and besieged Orléans, but Aetius allied with the Visigothic king Theodoric I and relieved the city. On 20 June 451 (traditional date) the armies clashed on the Catalaunian Plains, and Theodoric was killed. Attila withdrew, and Gaul stayed outside the Hun empire.

events.text: Invasion of Italy; Aquileia razed
events.detail: Attila returned in 452 to press his claim to Honoria, this time invading Italy over the Julian Alps. His army sacked many cities in the north and razed Aquileia so completely that its site was afterwards hard to recognise. Valentinian III sent envoys, including Pope Leo I, who met Attila near Mantua. Attila agreed to withdraw; his army was probably also weakened by famine and disease, and an eastern Roman force was attacking the Hun homeland. The invasion caused great destruction, but Italy stayed Roman and the Huns gained no territory there.

events.text: Attila dies; his sons divide the empire
events.detail: Early in 453 Attila died on the night of his wedding to a young bride, Ildico. According to the historian Priscus he suffered a severe nosebleed and choked in a drunken stupor. His empire had depended on his personal authority over many subject peoples. Now his sons Ellac, Dengizich and Ernak quarrelled over the inheritance, and the subject kings were treated like property to be shared out. Jordanes wrote that in their eagerness to rule the sons destroyed the empire, which began to break apart almost at once.

events.text: c. 454: Subject peoples defeat the Huns at the Nedao
events.detail: The subject peoples refused to be divided up like slaves. Led by Ardaric, king of the Gepids, who had been one of Attila's most loyal allies, a coalition of Gepids, Ostrogoths, Rugii, Heruli, Suebi and others rose in revolt. In about 454 they defeated the Huns in Pannonia at the river Nedao, whose location is unknown. According to Jordanes some 30,000 men fell, and Attila's eldest son Ellac was killed. The Huns lost control of the Hungarian Plain, and by the early 460s the former subjects had become independent kingdoms, many of them allied to Rome.

events.text: Dengizich defeated and killed in Thrace; the Hunnic empire is gone
events.detail: After Nedao the remaining Huns split into small groups near the lower Danube and the Black Sea steppe. Attila's son Dengizich tried to win back land and subsidies. Beaten by the Ostrogoths at Bassianae in 468, he then threatened Thrace and refused to negotiate with the Roman commander Anagast, so war dragged on until 469, when Dengizich was defeated and killed. According to the chronicler Marcellinus Comes his head was displayed in Constantinople. With his death, Hun rule in Europe was finished, and the empire disappears from the map.

name: Byzantine Empire
summary: The eastern half of the Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, outlived the West and under Justinian I reconquered North Africa, Italy and southern Spain, reaching its greatest extent in 565. The Arab conquests of the 630s–640s stripped away Syria and Egypt; the Macedonian emperors recovered ground up to Basil II's conquest of Bulgaria, before Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia to the Turks. Sacked by the Fourth Crusade in 1204 and restored from Nicaea in 1261, the shrunken state fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

events.text: Theodosius I dies; Arcadius rules the East from Constantinople
events.detail: For decades the Roman Empire had often been ruled by more than one emperor, each with his own court. Theodosius I was the last man to rule both halves, and when he died at Milan on 17 January 395, his two young sons, already co-emperors, divided the empire between them. Arcadius took the East, ruling from Constantinople, and Honorius the West. The split was meant to be administrative, but it proved permanent. This is where the map begins: the Eastern Roman Empire, later called Byzantine, covering the Balkans, Anatolia, Syria and Egypt.

events.text: Last western emperor deposed; Constantinople is the sole Roman capital
events.detail: By the 470s the Western Roman Empire had shrunk to little more than Italy, run by Germanic generals who set up puppet emperors. In 476 the barbarian commander Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna and did not name a successor. Instead, the Senate sent the imperial regalia to the eastern emperor Zeno, and Odoacer ruled Italy as king while nominally accepting Zeno as his superior. From now on the emperor in Constantinople was the only Roman emperor, and the East carried on Rome's traditions alone.

events.text: Belisarius defeats the Vandals and retakes North Africa (533–534)
events.detail: Justinian I, emperor from 527, wanted to win back the western provinces lost to Germanic kingdoms. In 530 the pro-Roman Vandal king Hilderic was overthrown by his cousin Gelimer, giving Justinian his excuse. A fleet under the general Belisarius landed in North Africa in September 533, routed the Vandals at Ad Decimum, near Carthage, and took the city. After a second victory at Tricamarum in December, Gelimer surrendered in spring 534. Africa, roughly modern Tunisia and coastal Algeria and Libya, was restored to the empire, the first big step in Justinian's reconquest.

events.text: Gothic War ends; Italy is back under Roman rule
events.detail: Next Justinian turned to Italy, ruled by the Ostrogoths. Belisarius invaded in 535 and took the Gothic capital Ravenna in 540, but a Gothic revival under King Totila dragged the war on for years. The eunuch general Narses finally crushed the Goths in the early 550s and drove back a Frankish invasion in 554, the year Justinian issued a decree setting up Italy's new government. Italy was back under Roman rule, but the long war had left it devastated. Only 14 years later the Lombards invaded and seized much of the peninsula.

events.text: Justinian I dies with the empire at its greatest extent
events.detail: Justinian died on 14 November 565, childless, after a 38-year reign. Besides Africa and Italy, his forces had also taken a strip of southern Spain, so the empire now ringed much of the Mediterranean again. He left lasting monuments too: the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople and the Corpus Juris Civilis, a code of Roman law that is still the basis of civil law in many countries. But the wars, and the plague of the 540s, which Justinian himself caught and survived, had drained the treasury. The map shows the empire at its widest here, and it soon began to shrink.

events.text: Heraclius defeats the Persians at Nineveh
events.detail: After the Persian king Khosrow II went to war against the empire in 602, over twenty years the Persians took Syria, Jerusalem and, for the first time, Egypt. The emperor Heraclius fought back from 622, and in late 627 he invaded Mesopotamia in a risky winter campaign. On 12 December 627 near the ruins of Nineveh he defeated a Persian army whose general, Rhahzadh, was killed. The Persians overthrew Khosrow, and the peace that followed returned all the lost provinces and the True Cross. Both empires, though, were now exhausted.

events.text: Arab victory at the Yarmuk ends Byzantine rule in Syria
events.detail: Only a few years after defeating Persia, the empire faced a new enemy: Arab armies united under Islam. They invaded Syria in the 630s, and in May 636 Heraclius sent a huge army to drive them out. The Arabs pulled back and gathered on the plains by the Yarmuk river, near today's borders of Syria, Jordan and Israel. In six days of fighting in August 636 they defeated the larger Byzantine force, in what became the greatest victory of their commander Khalid ibn al-Walid. Byzantine rule in Syria effectively ended, and the empire's frontier fell back to the Taurus Mountains of Anatolia.

events.text: Alexandria surrenders to the Arabs; Egypt lost
events.detail: In December 639 the Arab general Amr ibn al-As invaded Egypt, the empire's richest province and a main source of grain for Constantinople. He beat a Byzantine army at Heliopolis in 640 and took the Babylon Fortress, near modern Cairo, in 641. Alexandria, Egypt's capital, agreed to surrender by a treaty of November 641, and Arab troops entered the city the following September. The loss of Egypt cut off a huge share of the empire's revenue. The empire on the map was now reduced mainly to Anatolia, the Balkan coasts, parts of Italy and North Africa.

events.text: Leo III repels the Arab siege of Constantinople (717–718)
events.detail: In 716 a huge Umayyad army under Maslama, the caliph's brother, invaded Anatolia, hoping to exploit a Byzantine civil war. The general Leo III seized the throne in 717, just before the Arabs began a land and sea blockade of Constantinople behind its massive Theodosian Walls. The Byzantine navy used Greek fire, an incendiary liquid, to destroy much of the Arab fleet, so the city could be supplied by sea. A harsh winter, famine and disease, plus Bulgar attacks, wrecked the besiegers, who withdrew on 15 August 718. The capital, and Anatolia behind it, survived.

events.text: Basil II completes the conquest of Bulgaria
events.detail: Under its Tsar Samuel, the Bulgarian state had grown to stretch from the Adriatic to the Black Sea, and Emperor Basil II spent decades at war with it. On 29 July 1014 he trapped the Bulgarian army at Kleidion. According to chroniclers he blinded some 15,000 prisoners, leaving one man in every hundred with one eye to lead the rest home, and Samuel died of a stroke soon after. Bulgaria fought on until 1018, when it submitted. The empire's border reached the Danube again, and Basil earned the name 'Bulgar-Slayer'.

events.text: Seljuks capture Romanos IV at Manzikert; Normans take Bari
events.detail: In 1071 the empire suffered two blows at opposite ends. In the west, Norman adventurers captured Bari, the last Byzantine stronghold in southern Italy, ending centuries of rule there. In the east, Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes marched against the Seljuk Turks and met Sultan Alp Arslan near Manzikert, in eastern Anatolia, on 26 August 1071. Many of his troops fled, and Romanos became the only Byzantine emperor captured by a Muslim commander. Civil war followed his release, and Turkish groups poured into Anatolia, the empire's heartland.

events.text: Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople; empire splits into rump states
events.detail: The Fourth Crusade set out in 1202 to attack Egypt but could not pay Venice for its fleet. In exchange, the crusaders first sacked the Christian city of Zara, then sailed to Constantinople to put a Byzantine claimant, Alexios IV, on the throne in return for huge payments he could not make. In April 1204 they stormed the city and plundered its enormous wealth. A Latin Empire was set up there, while Greek rulers held on in three rump states centred on Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond. On the map the empire breaks apart, with the exiled court at Nicaea standing in for it.

events.text: Michael VIII of Nicaea recaptures Constantinople
events.detail: The Empire of Nicaea, in western Anatolia, became the strongest Greek successor state, and its ruler Michael VIII Palaiologos aimed to retake Constantinople. In July 1261 the general Alexios Strategopoulos was sent near the city with about 800 soldiers, mostly Cumans. On the night of 24–25 July they slipped in through the walls, and the Latin emperor Baldwin II fled by ship. Michael entered the city on 15 August and was crowned in Hagia Sophia. The Byzantine Empire was restored, but it was poorer and smaller than before 1204.

events.text: Ottomans take Adrianople as they push into the Balkans
events.detail: The Ottoman Turks, from north-west Anatolia, crossed into Europe after seizing Gallipoli in 1354, helped by Byzantine civil wars. Sultan Murad I's forces then conquered much of Thrace, and Adrianople (Edirne), the main city between Constantinople and the Balkans, fell in the 1360s. The date is disputed (some historians say 1361 or 1362, others about 1369), and the city became the Ottoman capital. Constantinople was now surrounded by Ottoman land, and by the 1370s the shrunken empire had become an Ottoman vassal.

events.text: Mehmed II takes Constantinople; Constantine XI dies
events.detail: By 1453 the empire was little more than Constantinople and a few lands in Greece. The young Sultan Mehmed II besieged the city from 6 April with an army far larger than its defenders. Huge cannons battered the ancient walls, and on 29 May 1453, after a 53-day siege, the Ottomans broke in, and the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, died in the fighting. Mehmed made Constantinople his new capital in place of Adrianople. The Byzantine Empire, the last direct heir of Rome, disappears from the map.

name: Tang China
summary: Founded in 618 by Li Yuan amid the collapse of the Sui (the map starts in 623), the Tang destroyed the Eastern Turks, conquered the Tarim Basin and, with Silla, Goguryeo, pushing protectorates as far as Central Asia. Defeat at Talas (751) and the An Lushan rebellion (755–763) ended this expansion, after which Tibet and regional governors ate into Tang power. The Huang Chao rebellion devastated the empire and the last emperor was deposed in 907.

events.text: Xuanwu Gate Incident: Li Shimin seizes power as Emperor Taizong
events.detail: The Tang dynasty was founded in 618 by Emperor Gaozu. His eldest son, Li Jiancheng, was crown prince, but the second son, Li Shimin, had won most of the battles that brought the family to power, and their rivalry turned deadly. On 2 July 626 Li Shimin and his men ambushed Li Jiancheng and another brother, Li Yuanji, at the Xuanwu Gate of the palace in Chang'an and killed them both. About two months later Gaozu abdicated, and Li Shimin became Emperor Taizong. Under his rule the Tang began its great expansion beyond China's borders.

events.text: Tang armies destroy the Eastern Turkic Khaganate
events.detail: Early in Taizong's reign the Eastern Turkic Khaganate, a nomad power on the Mongolian steppe, threatened the Tang frontier. Its ruler, Illig Qaghan, faced revolts by subject tribes and the defection of his own nephew. In the winter of 629 the Tang general Li Jing launched a surprise attack and destroyed the khan's camp, and in 630 Illig was captured and handed over. The Eastern Turks were resettled along the Yellow River as a buffer, and Taizong took the title of 'Heavenly Khagan'. Tang power now reached across the steppe of Inner Mongolia.

events.text: Conquest of Gaochang (Turfan); Anxi Protectorate set up
events.detail: Gaochang (Karakhoja), near Turfan in today's Xinjiang, was an oasis kingdom on the Silk Road that had sided with the Western Turks against the Tang. In 640 Taizong sent the general Hou Junji, who defeated the kingdom, and it was annexed as a Chinese prefecture. That same year the Tang set up the Protectorate General to Pacify the West (Anxi), first at Turfan. Its army later took Karashahr and Kucha, and the Four Garrisons of Anxi were set up from 648 onwards. The Tang now controlled the Silk Road into the Tarim Basin.

events.text: Western Turks defeated at Issyk Kul; protectorates reach Herat
events.detail: The Western Turkic Khaganate ruled the steppes and oases between the Tarim Basin and Persia. In 657 the Tang general Su Dingfang crushed the army of its khagan, Ashina Helu, and captured him (one source places the victory at Issyk Kul, another on the Irtysh river). The Tang set up protectorates over the Western Turks' lands, extending Chinese influence as far as Herat in Afghanistan. By the end of 657 the Tang had reached its largest extent.

events.text: Goguryeo destroyed by Tang and Silla
events.detail: The Korean kingdom of Goguryeo had beaten back Tang invasions in 645–648. The Tang then allied with Silla, a rival Korean kingdom, and after conquering Baekje together in 660 they attacked Goguryeo from north and south. Weakened by years of war and by quarrels among the sons of its late dictator, Goguryeo finally fell in late 668, when its capital Pyongyang was taken. The Tang set up a protectorate in its lands, pushing the map into northern Korea. Silla soon fought the Tang over the spoils, and within a decade it had driven the Chinese out of most of the peninsula.

events.text: Tibet seizes the Tarim Basin garrisons (held until 692)
events.detail: The Tibetan Empire was expanding north from the high plateau and competing with the Tang for the Silk Road oases. In 670 the Tibetans defeated a large Chinese army at the Dafei river, near Koko Nur, and with Khotanese help attacked the Tang's garrisons in the western Tarim Basin. The Chinese abandoned the region, and Tibet took control of all Four Garrisons of Anxi, ending two decades of Chinese rule. The Tang only won them back in 692. On the map, the Tang's long western arm into Central Asia is cut off for over twenty years.

events.text: Wu Zetian proclaims her own Zhou dynasty (690–705)
events.detail: Wu Zhao rose from a junior concubine to become empress of Emperor Gaozong, and after his death in 683 she ruled through her sons as empress dowager. In 690 she pushed her son aside, proclaimed her own Zhou dynasty in place of the Tang and took the title of emperor. She is the only woman in Chinese history to do so. She ruled largely from Luoyang, which she raised to co-capital, until the Shenlong Coup of 705 forced her from power and restored the Tang. The empire's borders stayed largely the same, so on the map the change is in name only.

events.text: Xuanzong begins a 44-year reign, the height of the Tang
events.detail: Xuanzong (Li Longji) became emperor in 712, after helping to remove rivals at court. His reign of 44 years was the longest of the dynasty. Its first decades, the Kaiyuan era (713–741), are seen as a golden age of stability, prosperity and culture, the age of poets such as Li Bai and Du Fu. To defend the long frontiers, Xuanzong created powerful military governors (jiedushi) who commanded large armies. That system kept the empire at its height on the map, but it also gave generals like An Lushan the power to rebel later.

events.text: Abbasid army defeats Gao Xianzhi at Talas
events.detail: Tang armies under the general Gao Xianzhi had pushed deep into Central Asia, as far as the Pamirs and the Tashkent area. At the same time the new Abbasid Caliphate was taking control of Khurasan and Transoxiana. In 751, near the Talas river on the border of today's Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, the Abbasid army under Ziyad ibn Salih, joined by Karluk Turks, defeated Gao. The battle marked the western limit of Tang expansion. Chinese rule in Central Asia ended soon after, though mainly because of the An Lushan rebellion that began four years later.

events.text: An Lushan rebels; the court flees Chang'an
events.detail: An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent, commanded three frontier armies in the north and was a favourite at Xuanzong's court. On 16 December 755 he rebelled, marching out of Fanyang, near modern Beijing, and taking Luoyang the next month. He declared his own Yan dynasty, and in 756 his forces broke through the mountain passes, and Xuanzong fled Chang'an for Sichuan. On the way his guards forced the death of his beloved consort Yang Guifei, and Xuanzong soon abdicated. The Tang had lost both its capitals, and its armies were pulled back from the frontiers.

events.text: Rebellion ends; Tibetans briefly occupy Chang'an; the west is lost
events.detail: After An Lushan was murdered in 757, his ally Shi Siming and then Shi's son carried on the war. It finally ended in early 763, when the last rebel leader was defeated, with help from Uyghur allies. But the Tang had stripped its western garrisons to fight, and the Tibetans moved in, seizing the Hexi Corridor and the lands of Gansu and Qinghai. Late in 763 they even captured Chang'an for 15 days, and the Tang survived, but much weaker. On the map it loses its Central Asian lands for good, and its provinces fall into the hands of semi-independent military governors.

events.text: Huang Chao rebellion begins (874–884), sacking Chang'an and Luoyang
events.detail: By the 870s the Tang faced famine, heavy taxes and widespread banditry. Huang Chao, a salt smuggler who had failed the state examinations, joined a rebellion led by Wang Xianzhi in the mid-870s and soon led his own army. He marched across China, sacking Guangzhou in the south in 878–879, then took Luoyang in 880 and Chang'an at the start of 881, where he declared himself emperor. Driven out in 883 by Tang forces led by the Shatuo Turk Li Keyong, he died in 884. The rebellion wrecked what was left of Tang authority, and warlords now held real power.

events.text: Zhu Wen deposes Emperor Ai and founds the Later Liang
events.detail: Zhu Wen was a former lieutenant of Huang Chao who changed sides in 882 and became a powerful military governor based at Kaifeng. By 903 he controlled the court, and he moved the emperor to Luoyang in 904, then had Emperor Zhaozong murdered and put the boy Emperor Ai on the throne. In 907 he forced Ai to give up the throne and declared himself emperor of a new Later Liang dynasty, and later had Ai killed. The Tang dynasty was over. China split into the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, and the Tang disappears from the map.
