name: Tibetan Empire
summary: Under Songtsen Gampo (r. c. 618–650) the Yarlung kings united the Tibetan Plateau, moved their seat to Lhasa and absorbed Zhangzhung and the Tuyuhun. Tibet contested the Tarim Basin with Tang China for two centuries, briefly occupied Chang'an in 763 and reached its greatest extent in the early 800s. After the murder of Ralpachen (838) and the assassination of Langdarma in 842 the empire broke apart.

events.text: Princess Wencheng leaves China to marry Songtsen Gampo
events.detail: Songtsen Gampo had united the clans of central Tibet and built a military power that threatened China's western frontier. After he attacked the Tuyuhun and the Chinese border town of Songzhou, demanding a royal bride, the Tang court agreed in 640 to a marriage alliance. Princess Wencheng, from a minor branch of the imperial family, then travelled to Tibet (sources date her departure to 640 or 641). The marriage brought peace and recognition for the young empire. Tibetan tradition credits her, with the king's Nepali wife Bhrikuti, with helping to bring Buddhism to Tibet.

events.text: c. 645: Songtsen Gampo overruns the kingdom of Zhangzhung
events.detail: Zhangzhung was an ancient kingdom in western Tibet, around Mount Kailash, ruled by the Lig myi dynasty. Songtsen Gampo married his sister to its king, Lig-myi-rhya, and when the king neglected her, she helped her brother defeat him. The date is disputed: Chinese annals say Zhangzhung submitted by 634, the scholar Rolf Stein places the conquest in 645, and some think it came only under Trisong Detsen a century later. Its conquest extended the empire far to the west across the plateau.

events.text: Tibet conquers the Tuyuhun (Azha) kingdom around Koko Nur
events.detail: The Tuyuhun, or Azha, were a kingdom of Xianbei origin around Lake Koko Nur (Qinghai), controlling key trade routes between Tibet and China. Songtsen Gampo had already raided them in the 630s, and they served as a buffer between Tibet and the Tang. In 663, under the powerful minister Gar Tongtsen, who ran the government for the young king, the Tibetan army defeated the Tuyuhun, who were gradually absorbed. With Koko Nur in Tibetan hands, the empire now bordered China directly in the north-east, which set up decades of war with the Tang.

events.text: Tibet takes the Tang's Four Garrisons in the Tarim Basin
events.detail: Pushing north from the plateau, Tibet wanted the rich Silk Road oases of the Tarim Basin, guarded by the Tang's Four Garrisons of Anxi. Between 665 and 670 it brought Khotan under its control. In the spring of 670 Tibetan armies, with Khotanese troops, captured Aksu, and the Chinese abandoned the region. The same year Tibet routed a large Tang army at the Dafei river near Koko Nur. Tibet now held all Four Garrisons, ending two decades of Chinese control, and the map stretches north across the Kunlun Mountains into today's Xinjiang.

events.text: Tang China regains the Tarim Basin
events.detail: Tibet held the Tarim Basin for 22 years, but its grip depended on alliances with Western Turkic tribes and on the loyalty of the oasis cities. Under Empress Wu, the Tang sent a fresh army west, and in 692 Chinese forces retook the Four Garrisons of Anxi, including Kucha and Khotan. Tibet's northern frontier fell back to the Kunlun Mountains. The two empires went on fighting for these oases for another half century, and by 750 the Tibetans had lost almost all their Central Asian possessions.

events.text: Nanzhao in Yunnan comes under Tibetan control (to 794)
events.detail: Nanzhao was a kingdom in Yunnan, in south-western China, with its capital near Dali. In 750 its king Geluofeng quarrelled with the local Chinese governor and went to war with the Tang, and he defeated large Chinese armies in 751 and 754. To protect himself he allied with Tibet, which treated Nanzhao as a vassal. The Tibetan Empire article says Nanzhao remained under Tibetan control from 750 to 794. The alliance extended Tibetan influence far to the south-east and let the two powers fight China together.

events.text: Trisong Detsen is crowned; the empire grows again
events.detail: In 756 the prince Song Detsen, then about 13, was crowned with the name Trisong Detsen after a period of turmoil at court. He became one of Tibet's greatest rulers. With the Tang crippled by the An Lushan rebellion, he pushed deep into Chinese territory and won back influence in Central Asia. He also invited Indian Buddhist teachers such as Padmasambhava and Shantarakshita, who built Samye, Tibet's first monastery. Under him the empire grew larger than ever before, with Tibetan armies holding much of today's Gansu and Qinghai.

events.text: Tibetans capture the Tang capital Chang'an for 15 days
events.detail: The An Lushan rebellion forced the Tang to pull its frontier armies back to defend the heartland, and the Tibetans swept into the undefended lands of the north-west. In late 763 a Tibetan army under the general Takdra Lukhong reached the Tang capital Chang'an, which the emperor Daizong had fled. The Tibetans occupied the city for fifteen days and installed a puppet emperor before withdrawing. The raid showed how far the balance had shifted. Tibet went on to hold the Hexi Corridor, cutting the Tang off from Central Asia.

events.text: Treaty with the Tang defines the frontier
events.detail: After decades of fighting, Tibet and the weakened Tang made a peace treaty in 783 that fixed the frontier between them, in Tibet's favour. It confirmed Tibetan control of large areas of today's Gansu, Qinghai and western Sichuan that the empire had taken since the 750s. The peace did not last long, as fighting broke out again within a few years. Still, the treaty marks the high point of Tibetan power. On the map the empire now reaches deep into what had been Chinese territory.

events.text: Nanzhao turns on Tibet and helps China defeat it at Shenchuan
events.detail: Nanzhao had been Tibet's ally and vassal since the 750s, but Tibetan demands for troops and tribute grew heavy. In 794 the Nanzhao king Yimouxun switched sides to the Tang. He attacked the Tibetans at Shenchuan and helped the Chinese inflict a serious defeat on them. Nanzhao and the Tang kept up the pressure, beating off Tibetan counterattacks in 799 and 801. Tibet lost its foothold in Yunnan, and its south-eastern frontier pulled back.

events.text: c. 812: Tibet's governor of Kabul submits to the Abbasids
events.detail: Under Tride Songtsen (Sadnalegs), Tibet fought a long war with the Abbasid Caliphate on its far western frontier. Tibetan forces were active as far west as Samarkand and Kabul, and the Tibetans had a governor in Kabul. As Abbasid forces gained the upper hand, this governor submitted to the caliphate and became a Muslim, in about 812 or 815 (the sources differ). Tibet lost its grip on Kabul and the Hindu Kush, and its western expansion came to an end.

events.text: Sino-Tibetan peace treaty (821/822), later inscribed in Lhasa
events.detail: Both Tibet and the Tang were worn down by more than a century of war, and both faced threats from the Uyghurs to the north. Under King Ralpachen (Tritsuk Detsen) the two empires agreed a peace treaty in 821–822. It confirmed the borders, and a bilingual text in Tibetan and Chinese was later carved on a stone pillar that still stands outside the Jokhang temple in Lhasa. The treaty brought peace for more than two decades and fixed the empire's eastern frontier at its greatest extent.

events.text: Ralpachen is murdered; his brother Langdarma takes the throne
events.detail: Ralpachen was a devoted patron of Buddhism who gave monks great privileges, which angered nobles loyal to the older Bön religion. In 838 he was murdered, either by his younger brother Langdarma or by two pro-Bön ministers who then placed Langdarma on the throne. Langdarma's reign was plagued by trouble. Tibetan Buddhists remember him for persecuting monks and nuns and destroying monasteries. Imperial patronage of Buddhism, which had lasted about eighty years, came to an end.

events.text: Langdarma assassinated; the empire disintegrates
events.detail: In 842 Langdarma was assassinated, traditionally by a Buddhist monk, Lhalung Pelgyi Dorje (some sources date the killing to 846). His death left a disputed succession between two young heirs, Yumtän and Ösung, backed by rival factions. Civil war broke out, and the empire dissolved into competing lordships, beginning Tibet's Era of Fragmentation. The Tibetan Empire disappears from the map, and its frontier lands in Gansu and Central Asia were lost over the following years.

name: Rashidun and Umayyad Caliphates
summary: After Muhammad's death in 632 the first caliphs, ruling from Medina, united Arabia and within twenty years took Syria and Egypt from Byzantium and destroyed the Sasanian Empire. From 661 the Umayyads ruled from Damascus and pushed the conquests to Spain, Sindh and Central Asia, creating one of the largest empires yet seen (c. 11 million km² by 720). Defeats at Constantinople (718) and Tours (732), the Berber revolt and civil wars sapped the dynasty, and the Abbasids overthrew it in 750.

events.text: Ridda wars over; Arabia united under Abu Bakr
events.detail: When the Prophet Muhammad died in June 632, his companion Abu Bakr was chosen as the first caliph, or successor. Many Arabian tribes then refused to pay taxes to Medina, and several rival prophets, such as Musaylima, gathered followers. Abu Bakr sent armies, the most famous led by Khalid ibn al-Walid, which won every campaign, and Musaylima was killed at the Battle of Yamama. By June 633 the Ridda ('apostasy') wars were over and all of Arabia was united under Medina. The new state could now turn its forces outward, against the Byzantine and Persian empires.

events.text: Victory at the Yarmuk delivers Syria to the Muslims
events.detail: Arab armies invaded Byzantine Syria in the 630s and took Damascus. In 636 Emperor Heraclius sent a huge army to drive them out. The Muslims pulled back and gathered on the plains by the Yarmuk river, near today's borders of Syria, Jordan and Israel. In six days of fighting in August 636, commanded by Khalid ibn al-Walid, they defeated the larger Byzantine force. Byzantine rule in Syria was effectively over, and the caliphate's map now pushes north from Arabia through Palestine and Syria to the Taurus Mountains.

events.text: Jerusalem surrenders to Caliph Umar
events.detail: After the Yarmuk, the Muslim commander Abu Ubayda besieged Jerusalem in November 636. After about six months the city's leader, Patriarch Sophronius, agreed to surrender, but only to the caliph in person. Caliph Umar travelled from Medina to receive the city's submission, in 637 or 638 (sources differ). According to tradition he guaranteed the safety of its Christian inhabitants and their churches. Jerusalem, holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims, was now part of the caliphate, along with the rest of Palestine.

events.text: Alexandria surrenders; Egypt conquered
events.detail: In December 639 the general Amr ibn al-As invaded Egypt, Byzantium's richest province, with about 4,000 men, later reinforced. He defeated a Byzantine army at Heliopolis in 640 and took the great Babylon Fortress, near modern Cairo, in 641. Alexandria agreed to surrender by a treaty in November 641, and Arab troops entered it in September 642. Amr founded a new capital, Fustat, near the old fortress. Egypt's grain and taxes now flowed to the caliphate, whose map stretched along the Nile and toward North Africa.

events.text: Sasanian army crushed at Nahavand
events.detail: After losing Mesopotamia and his capital Ctesiphon to the Arabs, the Persian king Yazdegerd III raised a new army in the Iranian highlands. In 642 it met the Arab forces under al-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin at Nahavand, south of Hamadan. The Persians were crushed, although Nu'man was reportedly killed in the final melee. The Sasanian imperial army effectively dissolved, and cities such as Isfahan soon fell. Persia lay open, and Yazdegerd fled east toward Merv.

events.text: Conquest of Persia completed; Yazdegerd III killed in Khurasan
events.detail: After Nahavand, Arab armies conquered the Iranian provinces one by one through the 640s. The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, fled from city to city, alienating local governors with his demands, and appealed in vain to Tang China for help. In 651 he was killed by a miller near Merv, possibly on the orders of the local governor. With him the 400-year-old Sasanian Empire ended. The caliphate's map now reached across all of Iran to Khurasan, on the edge of Central Asia.

events.text: Uthman murdered in Medina; Ali's accession starts the First Fitna
events.detail: Uthman, the third caliph, ruled from 644 and oversaw new conquests, but he was accused of favouring his own Umayyad clan with governorships and wealth. Rebels from Egypt and Iraq came to Medina, besieged his house and murdered him on 17 June 656. Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, was then chosen caliph. But Muhammad's widow Aisha and other leaders refused to accept him, and Mu'awiya, the Umayyad governor of Syria, demanded revenge for Uthman. The First Fitna (civil war) split the caliphate.

events.text: Ali killed; Mu'awiya founds the Umayyad dynasty at Damascus
events.detail: During the civil war Ali defeated Aisha's supporters at the Battle of the Camel in 656, but his clash with Mu'awiya at Siffin in 657 ended in stalemate and arbitration. Some of his own followers, the Kharijites, broke away in protest. In 661 a Kharijite, Ibn Muljam, assassinated Ali at Kufa, and his son Hasan soon abdicated. Mu'awiya was accepted as caliph and ruled from Damascus. He founded the Umayyad dynasty and, by naming his son as heir, made the caliphate hereditary.

events.text: Husayn killed at Karbala; Second Fitna follows
events.detail: When Mu'awiya died in 680, many refused to accept his son Yazid as caliph. Ali's son Husayn, grandson of the Prophet, set out for Kufa, whose people had invited him to lead a revolt. Umayyad troops intercepted his small band of about 72 men at Karbala, in Iraq. On 10 October 680 (10 Muharram) Husayn and most of his followers were killed. His death, mourned every year at Ashura, became central to Shia Islam and fed the Second Fitna, in which Ibn al-Zubayr declared himself caliph at Mecca and most provinces recognised him.

events.text: Abd al-Malik wins the civil war; Dome of the Rock completed
events.detail: After Yazid's death in 683, Umayyad power collapsed outside Syria, and most of the empire recognised Ibn al-Zubayr. The caliph Abd al-Malik, who came to power in 685, fought back. His forces retook Iraq in 691, and in 692 his general al-Hajjaj besieged Mecca and killed Ibn al-Zubayr. The Umayyads now ruled the whole caliphate again. In the middle of this war Abd al-Malik built the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed in 691–692, the oldest surviving great work of Islamic architecture.

events.text: Tariq ibn Ziyad invades Visigothic Spain; Sindh conquered
events.detail: With the empire reunited, the Umayyads expanded at both ends at once. In 711 Tariq ibn Ziyad, probably a Berber client of the governor Musa ibn Nusayr, crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic at Guadalete. Within a few years most of the Iberian Peninsula was under Muslim rule. In the same years (711–712) the young general Muhammad ibn al-Qasim conquered Sindh, in today's Pakistan, killing its king Dahir. The caliphate's map now stretched from the Atlantic to the Indus.

events.text: Siege of Constantinople (717–718) fails
events.detail: The Umayyads wanted to capture Constantinople, the Byzantine capital. In 716 a huge army and fleet under Maslama, the caliph's brother, invaded Anatolia, and in summer 717 they blockaded the city by land and sea. The Byzantines, led by the new emperor Leo III, destroyed much of the Arab fleet with Greek fire and kept the city supplied by sea. A harsh winter, famine, disease and Bulgar attacks wrecked the besiegers, who withdrew on 15 August 718. Byzantium survived, and the Taurus Mountains remained the frontier.

events.text: Frankish victory at Tours halts expansion in the west
events.detail: From Spain, Umayyad forces raided north into Gaul (France). In 732 the governor of al-Andalus, Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, defeated Duke Odo of Aquitaine and pushed toward Tours. On 10 October 732, somewhere between Poitiers and Tours, he met the Frankish army of Charles Martel and was killed, and his army withdrew. The battle is often said to have saved Western Europe, though historians debate how serious the threat was. Raids continued for some years, but the Pyrenees became the long-term northern limit of Muslim Spain.

events.text: Great Berber Revolt breaks out in North Africa
events.detail: Berbers in North Africa had converted to Islam and fought in the Arab armies, but Umayyad governors taxed them heavily and treated them as second-class Muslims. Inspired by egalitarian Kharijite preachers, they rose in revolt in Tangier, led at first by Maysara (the Umayyad Caliphate article dates the outbreak to 739, the Berber Revolt article to 740). The rebels crushed Arab armies, ending Umayyad rule in the western Maghreb, though the Umayyads held on to Ifriqiya (Tunisia) and Spain. Morocco and western Algeria broke away and never returned.

events.text: Abbasids defeat Marwan II at the Zab; Umayyad caliphate falls
events.detail: In the 740s the Umayyads were weakened by another civil war, while in Khurasan the Abbasid family, descendants of the Prophet's uncle al-Abbas, led a revolt under black banners. In January 750 the Abbasid army defeated the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, at the Great Zab river in northern Iraq. Damascus fell in April, Marwan was killed in Egypt in August, and most of the Umayyad family were massacred. The Umayyad caliphate was over. Only in Spain did an Umayyad prince later found a separate state.

name: Abbasid Caliphate
summary: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750, founded Baghdad in 762 and under al-Mansur, Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun presided over a vast empire and a golden age of learning. From the 9th century provinces broke away (Aghlabids, Tahirids, Tulunids, then the Fatimids), and after 945 the caliphs were figureheads under the Buyids and then the Seljuks; the map shows no Abbasid territory between 970 and 1201. Caliph al-Nasir revived a small state in Iraq, but the Mongols sacked Baghdad and killed the last caliph in 1258.

events.text: Abbasids defeat the Umayyads at the Zab; al-Saffah is caliph
events.detail: The Abbasids were descendants of al-Abbas, an uncle of the Prophet Muhammad, and claimed a better right to rule than the Umayyads. Their revolution began in Khurasan in June 747 under the Persian commander Abu Muslim, whose armies marched west under black banners. In Kufa they proclaimed Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah as caliph, and in January 750 his uncle Abdallah ibn Ali defeated the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, at the Great Zab river. The Abbasids inherited almost the whole Umayyad empire, from North Africa to Central Asia, and moved its centre from Syria to Iraq.

events.text: Abbasid victory over Tang China at Talas
events.detail: While the Abbasids were taking power, Tang China had pushed its armies deep into Central Asia under the general Gao Xianzhi. In 751 an Abbasid army led by Ziyad ibn Salih, joined by Karluk Turks, defeated the Tang force near the Talas river, on today's Kazakhstan–Kyrgyzstan border. The battle confirmed Muslim control of Transoxiana, the lands around Samarkand and Bukhara. Chinese prisoners are said to have brought papermaking to the Islamic world, though some historians doubt this. Tang power in the region soon collapsed anyway because of the An Lushan rebellion.

events.text: Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman sets up an independent al-Andalus
events.detail: Abd al-Rahman, a grandson of the Umayyad caliph Hisham, escaped the Abbasid massacre of his family in 750 and fled across North Africa, hiding among Berber tribes. In 755 he crossed to Spain, where many soldiers were still loyal to the Umayyads. In 756 he defeated the governor of al-Andalus and made himself emir at Córdoba, refusing to recognise the Abbasids. His dynasty ruled Muslim Spain for nearly three centuries. It was the first province to break away from the Abbasid Caliphate, and the Iberian Peninsula drops off the Abbasid map.

events.text: Al-Mansur founds Baghdad as the new capital
events.detail: In the early years the Abbasids governed from Kufa and other towns in Iraq, but they distrusted Kufa's support for rival claimants. The second caliph, al-Mansur, chose a site on the Tigris and began building a new capital in 762, a round city with walls and four gates, based on Persian designs. Chroniclers report that 100,000 workers took part. The Round City was finished by 766, and Baghdad grew into one of the largest cities in the world. It became a centre of trade and learning, home to the famous House of Wisdom.

events.text: Al-Ma'mun's forces take Baghdad, ending the civil war
events.detail: Caliph Harun al-Rashid named his son al-Amin as heir, with a second son, al-Ma'mun, to follow and to govern Khurasan. After Harun died in 809 the brothers fell out. In 811 al-Amin's army marched east, but al-Ma'mun's general Tahir ibn Husayn defeated it at Rayy and then besieged Baghdad. The city fell in September 813, al-Amin was killed, and al-Ma'mun became sole caliph. The main war was over, though unrest in Iraq went on until al-Ma'mun entered Baghdad in 819, and the long siege had badly damaged the capital.

events.text: Al-Mu'tasim moves the capital to Samarra
events.detail: Caliph al-Mu'tasim, ruling from 833, built his army around Turkic slave soldiers, whose presence caused clashes with the people of Baghdad. In 836 he founded a new capital and military base at Samarra, further up the Tigris. Later caliphs filled it with vast palaces and the Great Mosque with its spiral minaret, built in 847. Samarra remained the caliph's residence until 892, when the capital returned to Baghdad. The move kept the army apart from the city but left the caliphs dependent on their Turkic commanders.

events.text: Al-Mutawakkil murdered; the 'Anarchy at Samarra' begins
events.detail: In 861 Caliph al-Mutawakkil was murdered by his own Turkic guards. This began the 'Anarchy at Samarra' (861–870), when four caliphs in a row were made and unmade by rival army factions. Several were deposed or killed, and the Turkic troops even besieged Baghdad in 865–866. The anarchy ended in 870 with the accession of al-Mu'tamid. But the caliphs' prestige and treasury were badly damaged, and provincial governors began to act on their own, so that the empire on the map began to break up.

events.text: c. 870: Egypt becomes autonomous under Ahmad ibn Tulun
events.detail: Ahmad ibn Tulun was a Turkic slave-soldier sent to govern Egypt in 868. Within about four years he had made himself a virtually independent ruler, taking over Egypt's finances from the caliph's tax agent and built a large army loyal to himself. In 878 he also took control of Syria. His Tulunid dynasty ruled Egypt and Syria until 905, when the Abbasids briefly won them back. Egypt's wealth no longer flowed to Baghdad, and the caliphate's western provinces were slipping away.

events.text: Fatimids take Ifriqiya from the Aghlabids; North Africa lost
events.detail: The Fatimids were an Isma'ili Shia dynasty who claimed descent from the Prophet's daughter Fatima and rejected the Abbasids' right to rule. From 902 their missionary Abu Abdallah led Kutama Berber tribesmen against the Aghlabid emirs of Ifriqiya (Tunisia), who ruled in the Abbasids' name. In 909 he conquered Ifriqiya, and the Fatimid leader Abdallah al-Mahdi was proclaimed caliph. The Islamic world now had a rival Shia caliphate, and the last Abbasid foothold in North Africa west of Egypt was lost.

events.text: Buyids seize Baghdad; the caliphs become figureheads
events.detail: The Buyids were a Shia family from Daylam, in the mountains south of the Caspian Sea, who had built a state in western Iran. In 945 the youngest brother, Ahmad ibn Buya, took Baghdad and was given the title Mu'izz al-Dawla. From then on the Buyid emirs held real power in Iraq, while the Sunni Abbasid caliphs kept only a religious and ceremonial role. The caliphs no longer controlled any territory of their own. This is why the Abbasid map soon goes blank for more than two centuries.

events.text: Fatimids conquer Egypt and found Cairo
events.detail: Egypt was ruled by the Ikhshidid dynasty in the Abbasids' name, but by the 960s it was weakened by famine and infighting. In 969 the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz sent his general Jawhar with a large army from Ifriqiya. Jawhar crossed the Nile and took Fustat, Egypt's capital, in July 969, and soon began building a new capital nearby, Cairo. The Fatimids now ruled Egypt, and soon Palestine and parts of Syria as well. A rival caliph in Cairo now challenged Baghdad for leadership of the Muslim world.

events.text: Seljuk leader Tughril enters Baghdad, replacing the Buyids
events.detail: The Seljuks were Turkish nomads who had conquered Iran in the 1040s. In 1055 their leader Tughril entered Baghdad, pushed aside the Buyids and took the title of sultan. The caliph, al-Qa'im, kept his religious authority, but the Seljuk sultans now ran the government and the army. As Sunni Muslims, the Seljuks presented themselves as protectors of the Sunni caliph against the Shia Fatimids. The caliph still had no territory of his own, so the Abbasid map stays blank in this period.

events.text: Al-Nasir's long reign (to 1225) revives a caliphal state in Iraq
events.detail: As the Seljuk Empire weakened in the 12th century, the caliphs began to rebuild their own power, regaining control of Iraq under al-Muqtafi (r. 1136–1160). Al-Nasir, who ruled for 45 years from 1180 to 1225, went further. He expanded the caliph's state, extending his rule into parts of western Iran, and used diplomacy and religious brotherhoods to raise the caliph's prestige across the Muslim world. For the first time in over two centuries the Abbasids again ruled a real territorial state, which reappears on the map centred on Iraq.

events.text: Mongols under Hulagu sack Baghdad and execute al-Musta'sim
events.detail: In 1252 the Mongol Great Khan Möngke sent his brother Hulagu west with a huge army. After destroying the Assassins in Iran, Hulagu demanded that Caliph al-Musta'sim submit, and the caliph refused. The Mongols attacked Baghdad at the end of January 1258, the caliph surrendered on 10 February, and the city was sacked, with huge loss of life, and al-Musta'sim was killed. The Abbasid Caliphate of Baghdad, which had lasted five centuries, came to an end.

name: Carolingian Empire (Charlemagne)
summary: Pepin the Short replaced the Merovingians as king of the Franks in 751, and his son Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom, Saxony and the Avar lands, and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. After the civil war that followed Louis the Pious's death, the Treaty of Verdun (843) split the empire among his three sons. Charles the Fat reunited it in 884, but he was deposed in 887 and the empire dissolved for good on his death in 888.

events.text: Pepin the Short becomes king of the Franks
events.detail: For decades the Merovingian kings of the Franks had been figureheads, while real power lay with the 'mayors of the palace' of the Carolingian family. Pepin the Short, son of Charles Martel, held that office. In 751, with the support of Pope Zachary, he sent the last Merovingian king, Childeric III, to a monastery and had himself proclaimed King of the Franks, traditionally at Soissons. In 754 Pope Stephen II anointed him and his sons, and in return Pepin fought the Lombards and gave the pope lands in central Italy. This began the Carolingian dynasty.

events.text: Pepin dies; Charlemagne's rule begins
events.detail: Pepin died in September 768, and as was Frankish custom his kingdom was divided between his two sons, Charles (later called Charlemagne) and Carloman. The brothers did not get on, and civil war seemed possible. When Carloman died in 771, Charles took over his lands and became sole king. Carloman's widow and children fled to the Lombard king Desiderius, which helped set the two kingdoms against each other. Charlemagne went on to spend most of his 46-year reign at war, greatly enlarging the Frankish realm.

events.text: Saxon Wars begin; they last until 804
events.detail: The Saxons were pagan peoples living between the Rhine and the Elbe, in what is now northern Germany, who often raided Frankish lands. In 772 Charlemagne invaded Saxony and destroyed the Irminsul, a sacred pillar or tree the Saxons worshipped. The wars dragged on for 32 years, with repeated revolts led by the chieftain Widukind, who finally submitted and was baptised in 785. In 782, after a Saxon victory over a Frankish army, Charlemagne ordered 4,500 Saxon rebels beheaded at Verden. The conquest pushed the Frankish border east to the Elbe and spread Christianity by force.

events.text: Charlemagne conquers the Lombard kingdom of Italy
events.detail: The Lombards ruled northern and central Italy from their capital Pavia, and their king Desiderius threatened the pope's lands and sheltered the family of Charlemagne's late brother. Pope Hadrian I called on Charlemagne for help. In 773 Charlemagne crossed the Alps and besieged Pavia, which surrendered in June 774 after a long blockade. Desiderius was sent to a monastery, and Charlemagne took the title King of the Lombards. Northern and central Italy now joined the Frankish realm, and the map reaches south toward Rome.

events.text: Rearguard ambushed by Basques at Roncevaux
events.detail: In 778 Charlemagne accepted an invitation from Muslim governors in northern Spain who promised to submit to him if he helped them against the emir of Córdoba. His army crossed the Pyrenees, but the city of Zaragoza did not open its gates, and the campaign failed. On the way home he destroyed the walls of Pamplona, and in revenge Basques ambushed his rearguard in the Roncevaux Pass and wiped it out. Among the dead was the commander Roland, later the hero of the epic Song of Roland. Frankish expansion into Spain stalled for years.

events.text: Charlemagne campaigns against the Avars in Pannonia
events.detail: The Avars were a nomadic people who had ruled the Pannonian Basin (modern Hungary) since the 560s and grown rich on plunder and tribute. In summer 791 Charlemagne invaded their lands along the Danube while his son Pippin, King of Italy, attacked from the south-east. In 795 or 796 a Frankish force captured the khagan's fortified camp, the 'Ring', with much of its treasure, and in 796 the khagan submitted. By 803 the Avar khaganate was finished. Its western lands, in today's Austria and western Hungary, became part of the empire.

events.text: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor in Rome
events.detail: In 799 Pope Leo III, attacked by enemies in Rome, met Charlemagne at Paderborn to seek his protection, and Charlemagne later went to Rome, restored the pope, and on Christmas Day 800, in St Peter's Basilica, Leo crowned him emperor of the Romans. He was the first emperor in the West in over 300 years, which angered the Byzantine emperors in Constantinople, who saw themselves as the only Roman emperors. Though historians still debate its meaning, the coronation gave Charlemagne's realm the status of an empire, the Carolingian Empire.

events.text: Final Saxon campaign; Saxony absorbed
events.detail: Saxony had seemed conquered several times, but revolts kept breaking out, especially in the far north. In 798 Charlemagne's Slavic allies, the Obotrites, defeated the Nordalbingian Saxons north of the Elbe, and the Franks deported many Saxons to other parts of the empire. The last rising was put down in 804, more than 30 years after the first campaign. Saxony was now firmly part of the empire. The map's eastern frontier reached the Elbe, bordering Danes and Slavs.

events.text: Charlemagne dies at Aachen; Louis the Pious succeeds
events.detail: Charlemagne had made his son Louis co-emperor in 813, since two older sons had died. When Charlemagne died at his capital Aachen in January 814, Louis, later called 'the Pious', became sole emperor of the whole realm. Louis struggled to keep control, and his repeated plans to share the empire among his sons led to revolts in which they even imprisoned him. The empire kept its full size during his reign. Its unity, though, depended on a family that was already at war with itself.

events.text: Treaty of Verdun divides the empire among three brothers
events.detail: When Louis the Pious died in 840, his eldest son Lothair claimed the whole empire. His brothers Louis the German and Charles the Bald refused and defeated him at Fontenoy in 841. By the Treaty of Verdun, agreed on 10 August 843, the empire was split three ways: West Francia went to Charles, East Francia to Louis, and a long middle kingdom from the North Sea to Italy to Lothair, who kept the title of emperor. The division roughly foreshadowed the later shapes of France and Germany.

events.text: Treaty of Meerssen splits Lotharingia between East and West
events.detail: Lothair's middle kingdom was itself divided among his sons in 855. The northern part, Lotharingia (Lorraine), went to Lothair II, who died in 869 with no legitimate heir. His uncles Charles the Bald of West Francia and Louis the German of East Francia then split Lotharingia between them by the Treaty of Meerssen in 870. The middle kingdom disappeared, and its lands were added to West and East Francia. Lotharingia stayed a disputed borderland between France and Germany for centuries.

events.text: Charles the Fat reunites all the Frankish kingdoms
events.detail: After Charles the Bald died in 877, the Frankish kingdoms passed rapidly between short-lived kings, while Vikings raided in the north and west. Charles the Fat, a son of Louis the German, had inherited parts of East Francia and Italy and was crowned emperor in 881. When the young king of West Francia, Carloman, died in a hunting accident in 884, Charles inherited his lands as well. For the last time all the Frankish kingdoms were ruled by one man. On the map the empire of Charlemagne briefly reappears.

events.text: Charles buys off the Vikings besieging Paris
events.detail: Viking armies had been raiding along the rivers of West Francia for decades. In November 885 a large Viking force sailed up the Seine and besieged Paris, which Count Odo defended with only a few hundred soldiers. The city held out for months, and when Charles the Fat finally arrived with an army in 886, he did not fight. Instead he promised the Vikings 700 livres of silver and let them sail on up the Seine to raid Burgundy. Many nobles saw this as cowardly, and Charles's standing collapsed, while Odo's grew.

events.text: Charles the Fat deposed; the empire dissolves on his death in 888
events.detail: Charles the Fat was in poor health and was blamed for failing against the Vikings. In November 887 his nephew Arnulf of Carinthia rebelled, and the East Frankish nobles deposed Charles, who died in January 888. No Carolingian was strong enough to take the whole inheritance. Arnulf became king in East Francia, Count Odo of Paris was elected king of West Francia, and separate kings arose in Italy, Aquitaine and Burgundy. The Carolingian Empire dissolved for good and disappears from the map.

name: Ghana Empire (Wagadu)
summary: The Soninke kingdom of Ghana, between the Senegal and Niger rivers, grew rich on the trans-Saharan gold trade and was already known to Arab writers as the 'Land of Gold' in the 8th century. It peaked in the 10th–11th centuries, seized the trading town of Awdaghust in 990 and was described in detail by al-Bakri in 1068. Its rulers converted to Islam around 1076 (whether the Almoravids conquered it is disputed); weakened, it was overrun by the Sosso by 1203 and later absorbed into Mali.

events.text: Al-Khwarizmi makes the first known written mention of Ghana
events.detail: Ghana, or Wagadu, was a kingdom of the Soninke people in the western Sahel, in what is now south-eastern Mauritania and western Mali. 'Ghana' was really the title of its king, meaning war chief. Its origins may go back several centuries, but it had no writing of its own, so outsiders' accounts are our main sources. The first identifiable written mention of its ruling dynasty comes from the Baghdad scholar al-Khwarizmi in about 830, and Ghana appears on his world map. Arab writers already knew it as a wealthy 'land of gold' on the far side of the Sahara.

events.text: Ibn Hawqal calls Ghana's king the 'wealthiest king on earth'
events.detail: Ghana's power rested on trade across the Sahara. It controlled the routes that carried gold from mines to the south toward North Africa, and it imported salt from the desert in return. The Arab geographer Ibn Hawqal, writing in the 970s, called the king of Ghana the 'wealthiest king on the face of the earth' because of his stocks of gold. He also noted that Ghana depended on the Berber town of Awdaghust, on the desert edge, for salt. The map shows Ghana at its height as a trading empire between the desert and the Niger.

events.text: Ghana conquers Awdaghust and installs a governor
events.detail: Awdaghust (Aoudaghost), in what is now southern Mauritania, was a key caravan town at the southern end of a trade route across the Sahara, long controlled by Sanhaja Berbers. According to the Ghana Empire article, Ghana conquered it in 990, probably for commercial reasons, and installed its own governor. The article on the town says only that it became part of Ghana in the late 10th or early 11th century. Taking Awdaghust gave Ghana direct control of a northern trade terminus and pushed its power into the desert.

events.text: Almoravids capture Awdaghust
events.detail: In the early 1050s a new movement arose among the Sanhaja Berbers of the western Sahara: the Almoravids, led by the preacher Abdallah ibn Yasin and the Lamtuna chiefs, who preached a strict form of Islam. In 1054–55 they attacked and captured Awdaghust, then one of Ghana's royal seats. The Almoravids took control of the Saharan trade routes and soon conquered Morocco. Ghana lost its northern outpost, and a powerful, aggressive neighbour now stood on its desert frontier.

events.text: Tunka Manin succeeds Bassi as king
events.detail: Bassi, whom al-Bakri calls Ghana's king, died in 1063 and was succeeded by his nephew, Tunka Manin. Kingship traditionally passed to the son of the king's sister. Bassi and Tunka Manin are the only kings of Ghana known to us by name. Tunka Manin ruled a powerful state at war with the neighbouring kingdom of Silla, and he corresponded with the Almoravid leader Yusuf ibn Tashfin. Some historians think the succession caused a dispute with Bassi's son, which may have given the Almoravids a chance to meddle in Ghana's politics.

events.text: Al-Bakri describes the capital's royal and Muslim towns
events.detail: Al-Bakri, a scholar in Córdoba in Muslim Spain, completed his 'Book of Routes and Realms' in about 1068. He never visited Ghana but gathered information from earlier writers and travellers. He described the capital as two towns about six miles (10 km) apart: a large Muslim merchants' town with twelve mosques, and the king's town, al-Ghaba, where the king kept the traditional religion. Many of the king's ministers and interpreters were Muslims. The ruins of Koumbi Saleh in Mauritania are thought to be the merchants' town, although this is not certain.

events.text: c. 1076: Rulers convert to Islam; Almoravid conquest disputed
events.detail: An old tradition says the Almoravids conquered Ghana in 1076–77 and converted its people to Islam. Modern historians sharply question this. In 1982 the scholars Conrad and Fisher argued that no military conquest happened, and that the story comes from misreading Arabic sources written centuries later. What is clearer is that in this period Ghana's rulers became Muslims, perhaps under Almoravid pressure or influence. The kingdom survived, so the map keeps showing Ghana in the same place after this date.

events.text: Al-Idrisi describes Ghana as a powerful, fully Muslim kingdom
events.detail: The geographer al-Idrisi, working at the court of the Norman king Roger II of Sicily, completed his great description of the world in 1154. He described Ghana as a powerful, fully Muslim kingdom, whose rulers claimed descent from the Prophet's family. Some historians treat his account with caution because of errors in his geography. Still, it suggests Ghana had recovered and even enjoyed a second period of strength in the 12th century. That resurgence did not last: by about 1203 the Sosso had risen and conquered Ghana.

name: Khmer Empire
summary: Jayavarman II's consecration as universal monarch on Phnom Kulen in 802 founded the Angkorian empire, and Yasovarman I built the first capital at Angkor. Suryavarman II (builder of Angkor Wat) and Jayavarman VII (Angkor Thom, the Bayon) led its high point, including the conquest of Champa after the Cham sack of Angkor in 1177. From the 14th century the Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya pressed in, and Angkor was abandoned after its fall in 1431.

events.text: Jayavarman II proclaims himself universal monarch on Phnom Kulen
events.detail: Before 802, Cambodia was divided among rival Khmer princedoms that grew out of the older state of Chenla. A prince named Jayavarman II brought them together under his rule. In 802, on the sacred mountain of Mahendraparvata, now Phnom Kulen, he held a Hindu consecration ritual and proclaimed himself chakravartin, 'universal ruler', and a god-king. He also declared his kingdom independent of 'Java', which may mean the island of Java or a neighbouring power. Historians date the Khmer Empire from this ceremony, and it appears on the map centred on north-western Cambodia.

events.text: Yasovarman I founds Yasodharapura, the first city at Angkor
events.detail: Indravarman I had expanded the kingdom and built temples and reservoirs near the Tonle Sap lake. His son Yasovarman I, who came to the throne in 889, founded a new capital, Yasodharapura, the first city at Angkor. Its central temple stood on Phnom Bakheng, a hill about 60 metres high. He also built the East Baray, a huge reservoir about 7 km long. Angkor stayed the heart of the empire for more than five centuries, and its waterworks fed the rice fields that supported its people and armies.

events.text: Rajendravarman II returns the court to Angkor from Koh Ker
events.detail: In the early 10th century the court was moved away from Angkor. King Jayavarman IV built a new capital at Koh Ker, some 100 km to the north-east. In 944 Rajendravarman II came to the throne and brought the royal palace back to Yasodharapura at Angkor. He resumed great building projects there, including the Hindu temples of Pre Rup and the East Mebon, on an island in the East Baray. In 950 he fought the first recorded war with Champa, the kingdom to the east in today's central Vietnam, beginning centuries of conflict between the two.

events.text: Suryavarman I takes Angkor and reunites the kingdom
events.detail: After the death of Jayavarman V in 1001, rival kings fought over the throne. Suryavarman I defeated his opponents and took Angkor, becoming sole king (his reign is dated from 1002 or 1006, depending on the source). He made an alliance with the Chola Empire of south India against the Malay kingdom of Tambralinga. He pushed the empire west to Lopburi in the Chao Phraya basin of today's Thailand, and east along the Mekong, and began the West Baray, a reservoir 8 km long. The empire on the map now stretched well beyond Cambodia.

events.text: Suryavarman II begins his reign; Angkor Wat is built
events.detail: Suryavarman II came to the throne in 1113 and ruled until about 1150. He was an ambitious warrior who attacked Dai Viet, in northern Vietnam, several times without success, and fought Champa. He is best known as the builder of Angkor Wat, a vast temple dedicated to Vishnu and probably meant as his own mausoleum. It was built during his reign and is today the largest religious monument in the world. His reign marks a high point of Khmer power and art.

events.text: Suryavarman II sacks the Cham capital Vijaya
events.detail: Champa, the Cham kingdom on the coast of central Vietnam, was the Khmers' long-standing rival. Its king, Jaya Indravarman III, had refused to keep supporting Khmer attacks on Dai Viet. In 1145 Suryavarman II invaded Champa, defeated the king and sacked the Cham capital, Vijaya. He put a new king, Harideva, said to be his wife's younger brother, on the Cham throne. But the Chams soon fought back under Jaya Harivarman I, retook their capital and killed Harideva, and a final Khmer expedition in 1150 ended in a disastrous withdrawal.

events.text: Cham fleet sails up the Tonle Sap and sacks Angkor
events.detail: After Suryavarman II died, the Khmer court was weakened by struggles over the throne. In 1177 the Cham king Jaya Indravarman IV took revenge for earlier wars. His fleet sailed up the Mekong, across the great Tonle Sap lake and up the Siem Reap river to Angkor. The Chams pillaged the capital and killed the Khmer king, Tribhuvanadityavarman. It was the worst disaster in the empire's history so far, and for a few years the Khmer state was in chaos.

events.text: Jayavarman VII is crowned and builds Angkor Thom and the Bayon
events.detail: A Khmer prince, already in his fifties, led the fight to drive out the Cham invaders, including a naval battle carved on the walls of the Bayon temple. Having ended the factional fighting, he was crowned in 1181 as Jayavarman VII. He was the first Khmer king devoted to Buddhism. He rebuilt the capital as Angkor Thom, a walled city with the Bayon temple, famous for its giant stone faces, at its centre. He also built roads with rest houses and, according to inscriptions, 102 hospitals across the realm.

events.text: Khmer conquest of Champa (1190–1191)
events.detail: Jayavarman VII wanted revenge for the Cham sack of Angkor in 1177. In 1190 he sent his armies into Champa, helped by Sri Vidyanandana, a Cham prince who had taken refuge at the Khmer court. They sacked and conquered Champa in 1190–1191. The Khmers then installed their own rulers, and Champa remained a dependency of the Khmer Empire for about 30 years. The empire now reached the coast of central Vietnam, near its greatest extent on the map.

events.text: Jayavarman VIII begins paying tribute to the Mongols
events.detail: Jayavarman VIII, who reigned from 1243 to 1295, was a follower of Hindu Shaivism who destroyed many Buddhist statues. In 1283 the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty of China threatened Cambodia. To avoid war with the Mongol general Sogetu, Jayavarman VIII began paying annual tribute in 1285. The tribute kept the Mongols out, and the empire avoided invasion. But it also showed that the Khmers now had to bow to a stronger power, and his rule ended in 1295 when his son-in-law Srindravarman deposed him.

events.text: Chinese envoy Zhou Daguan finds Angkor ravaged by war with Siam
events.detail: In 1296 the Yuan emperor Temür Khan sent an embassy to Cambodia that included the diplomat Zhou Daguan. He arrived at Angkor in August 1296 and stayed until July 1297. He later wrote 'The Customs of Cambodia', the only detailed eyewitness account of daily life in Angkor. He recorded that in a recent war with the Siamese 'the country was utterly devastated'. The new Thai kingdoms to the west were beginning to eat into the empire's lands, which shrank on the map.

events.text: Ayutthaya besieges Angkor, taking it the next year
events.detail: In the 14th century the Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya, in the lower Chao Phraya valley, became the Khmers' main rival. In 1352 King Uthong of Ayutthaya besieged Angkor. The city was captured the next year, and the Khmer king was replaced with Siamese princes for several years. Ayutthaya also kept control of western Khmer provinces it had seized. The Khmers recovered their capital, but the balance of power had shifted west, and later Siamese attacks followed, including another capture of Angkor in the 1390s.

events.text: Angkor falls to Ayutthaya; the court moves to the Phnom Penh area
events.detail: Ayutthaya's armies besieged Angkor again, and according to Thai chronicles the city fell in 1431 after a siege of about seven months. The Khmer king Ponhea Yat judged Angkor indefensible and moved his court south, eventually to the area of present-day Phnom Penh. Angkor was not completely abandoned, and its temples remained in religious use. But the Angkorian empire was over, and historians mark this as the start of Cambodia's post-Angkor period.

name: Chola Empire
summary: Vijayalaya re-founded Chola power at Thanjavur around 848, and his successors overcame the Pandyas and Pallavas. Rajaraja I (985–1014) and Rajendra I (1014–1044) made it the leading power of South India and the Bay of Bengal, taking Sri Lanka and the Maldives, marching to the Ganges and raiding Srivijaya in 1025. The Later Cholas held most of the Tamil country after 1070, but Pandya attacks from 1215–16 broke the empire; the map ends in 1259, and the last king, Rajendra III, is last recorded in 1279.

events.text: Aditya I and the Pallavas defeat the Pandyas
events.detail: Around 850 the Chola chief Vijayalaya took Thanjavur, in the Kaveri delta, during a war between the Pallava and Pandya kingdoms. His son Aditya I at first fought as an ally of the Pallavas, the dominant power in the north of Tamil country. Together with the Pallava king Aparajita and the Western Ganga king, the Cholas defeated the Pandyas of Madurai at Thirupurambiyam (dated c. 885 in the Chola Empire article, 878 in Aditya's own article). The Cholas gained land as a reward. Aditya later turned on the Pallavas, killing Aparajita in battle and annexing their kingdom.

events.text: Parantaka I invades Sri Lanka
events.detail: Aditya's son Parantaka I continued the expansion. Early in his reign he captured Madurai and defeated a combined Pandya and Sri Lankan army, and the Pandya king fled to Sri Lanka with his royal regalia. When the Sinhalese king refused to hand them over, Parantaka attacked the island. The Chola Empire article dates the conquest to 925, while the article on Parantaka places the main invasion, which sacked Anuradhapura, around 946–947. Either way the Cholas could not hold the island, and its army returned to Anuradhapura once they left.

events.text: Defeat by the Rashtrakutas at Takkolam; Tondaimandalam lost
events.detail: In the north the Cholas faced the Rashtrakutas, the strongest power in the Deccan. Around 948–949 the Rashtrakuta king Krishna III and his Western Ganga ally Butuga II invaded and met a Chola force under the crown prince Rajaditya at Takkolam, near Kanchipuram. Rajaditya was killed on the battlefield, according to some accounts while riding an elephant, and the Cholas were defeated. They lost the northern province of Tondaimandalam, around Kanchipuram, to the Rashtrakutas. For the next three decades Chola power shrank back toward the Kaveri delta.

events.text: Rajaraja I takes the throne
events.detail: Arulmozhi Varman became king in 985 after the death of his uncle Uttama Chola, taking the name Rajaraja, 'king of kings'. He inherited a small kingdom around Thanjavur and Tiruchirappalli that was still recovering from the Rashtrakuta wars. Over nearly thirty years he built a powerful army and navy and conquered the Pandya and Chera kingdoms, the Deccan lands of Vengi and Gangavadi, and northern Sri Lanka. He also organised a land survey in 1000. Under him the Chola kingdom became an empire, and the map begins to spread across south India.

events.text: Chola forces invade the Anuradhapura kingdom of Sri Lanka
events.detail: The Sinhalese kingdom of Anuradhapura, in northern Sri Lanka, had fallen into chaos. Around 982 its army, largely Tamil mercenaries, revolted against King Mahinda V, who fled to Rohana in the south. Rajaraja I took advantage of the eleven years of disorder and invaded in 993. The Cholas took the north of the island, made Polonnaruwa their provincial capital and renamed it Jananathamangalam. For the first time the Chola map stretched across the Palk Strait into Sri Lanka.

events.text: Rajaraja dedicates the great Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur
events.detail: Rajaraja I built the Brihadisvara temple at his capital, Thanjavur, between 1003 and 1010, dedicating it to the god Shiva. It was the grandest temple of its age in south India. Its granite tower (vimana) over the shrine is one of the tallest in the region, and it houses one of the largest Shiva lingas in India. The temple displayed the wealth and power of the Chola state and served as a centre of worship, administration and the arts. Today it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Great Living Chola Temples'.

events.text: c. 1017: Rajendra completes the conquest of Sri Lanka's Rajarata
events.detail: Rajaraja's son Rajendra I, king from 1014, finished what his father began in Sri Lanka. According to the Sinhalese chronicle, the Mahavamsa, the conquest was completed in about 1017–1018. Rajendra's army marched into Rohana, the island's southern refuge, and captured King Mahinda V with his queen, his crown and great treasure, and also seized the Pandya regalia kept there. Mahinda died as a prisoner in India in 1029. All of Rajarata, the northern kingdom of Sri Lanka, was now a Chola province.

events.text: Rajendra's forces take the Maldives and Lakshadweep
events.detail: The Cholas had a strong navy and wanted to control the trade routes of the Indian Ocean. In 1018 Rajendra's forces captured the Maldives and the Lakshadweep (Laccadive) islands off the west coast of India. Rajendra renamed the islands 'Twelve Thousand Islands and the Ocean Where Three Waters Meet'. His father Rajaraja had already extended Chola influence over parts of the Maldives. The conquest gave the Cholas bases on the sea lanes between Arabia and South-East Asia, and the map reaches out into the Arabian Sea.

events.text: Ganges expedition returns; a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, follows
events.detail: Rajendra sent an army on a great campaign to the north, through Odisha and Bengal, where it defeated the Pala king and reached the river Ganges. The army returned around 1022 with water from the Ganges. Rajendra took the title Gangaikonda, 'he who took the Ganges', and built a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, with a great Shiva temple and a huge tank where the Ganges water was mixed. The northern lands were raided, not ruled. But the campaign showed Chola power from Sri Lanka to Bengal.

events.text: Naval raids on Srivijaya and Kedah
events.detail: Srivijaya, based on Sumatra, controlled the Strait of Malacca, the main sea route between India and China, and forced passing ships to use its ports. In 1025 Rajendra launched a swift naval invasion that took Srivijaya by surprise. His fleet attacked its ports, including Kedah (Kadaram) on the Malay Peninsula, and captured its king, Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman. The raid did not create lasting rule. But it broke Srivijaya's grip on the strait for a time and spread Chola influence into South-East Asia.

events.text: Kulottunga I founds the Later Cholas; overseas lands slip away
events.detail: In 1070 the Chola king Athirajendra was killed in a civil disturbance, leaving no heir. His cousin Kulothunga I, son of an Eastern Chalukya king of Vengi and grandson of Rajendra I through his mother, took the throne. He began the line known as the Later Cholas and ruled until 1122. He kept the core empire strong and claimed overlordship over Kedah, but the Cholas lost Sri Lanka to a revival of Sinhalese power, and they began to lose control of the Pandya lands. The map starts to shrink at its edges.

events.text: c. 1118: Vengi lost to the Chalukyas, Gangavadi to the Hoysalas
events.detail: Late in Kulothunga I's reign, around 1118, the Cholas suffered losses on their northern frontiers. The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani occupied Vengi, the Telugu coastal lands the Cholas had controlled through marriage alliances, and the Hoysalas under Vishnuvardhana took Gangavadi, in what is now southern Karnataka. These were temporary setbacks. Kulothunga's son Vikrama Chola soon recovered Vengi and part of Gangavadi. Still, they showed that new regional powers were rising around the empire.

events.text: c. 1216: Pandya king Maravarman Sundara defeats Kulottunga III
events.detail: Kulothunga III had defeated the Pandyas and in 1205 burned their coronation hall at Madurai. In 1216 a new Pandya king, Maravarman Sundara Pandyan, came to power determined to take revenge. He invaded the Chola kingdom, sacked Thanjavur and Uraiyur and drove the aged Kulothunga III and his heir into exile. Hoysala help won Kulothunga back his kingdom, but only as a Pandya vassal, and from now on the Cholas were weak and dependent. The Pandyas were the rising power in Tamil country, and they finally ended the Chola dynasty around 1279.

name: Holy Roman Empire
summary: Otto I's imperial coronation in 962 joined the German kingdom to Italy, and Burgundy was added in 1032, making the empire the strongest monarchy in western Europe into the 13th century. Clashes with the papacy and the collapse of Hohenstaufen power after 1250 left the princes increasingly independent, a system fixed by the Golden Bull of 1356 and the reforms of 1495. The Reformation and the Thirty Years' War further weakened imperial authority; Westphalia (1648) recognised the loss of Switzerland and the Dutch Netherlands, and Francis II dissolved the empire in 1806.

events.text: Pope John XII crowns Otto I emperor in Rome
events.detail: After the Carolingian Empire broke up, East Francia became a kingdom of German duchies. Otto I, Duke of Saxony and king from 936, made it the strongest power in Europe. In 955 he crushed the Magyars at the Lechfeld, ending their raids on the West, and by 961 he had conquered the Kingdom of Italy. Following Charlemagne's example, he was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope John XII in 962. Historians date the Holy Roman Empire from this coronation, which joined the German and Italian kingdoms under one emperor for centuries.

events.text: Kingdom of Burgundy joins Germany and Italy under the emperor
events.detail: Rudolph III, the childless king of Burgundy (a kingdom in the Rhône valley and western Alps, between France and Italy), had promised his throne to the German rulers. When he died in 1032, Emperor Conrad II, the first of the Salian dynasty, claimed the kingdom and conquered it with German and Italian troops, becoming its king in 1033. Burgundy, later known as the Kingdom of Arles, joined Germany and Italy as the third of the empire's 'three kingdoms'. On the map the empire now reached south to the Mediterranean coast of Provence.

events.text: Henry IV's Walk to Canossa during the Investiture Controversy
events.detail: Popes and emperors clashed over who had the right to appoint bishops, who were also powerful landholders. This was the 'Investiture Controversy'. When Pope Gregory VII tried to ban lay investiture, the German king Henry IV had his bishops reject the pope in 1076, and Gregory excommunicated and deposed him. With German nobles threatening revolt, Henry crossed the Alps in winter and in January 1077 came to Canossa Castle, where the pope was staying. According to contemporary sources he waited three days in the snow, in a penitent's hair shirt, before Gregory lifted the excommunication.

events.text: Concordat of Worms settles the investiture dispute
events.detail: The Investiture Controversy dragged on for decades after Canossa, through civil wars in Germany and fighting in Italy. Henry IV's son, Emperor Henry V, finally negotiated a compromise with Pope Callixtus II. By the Concordat of Worms, signed on 23 September 1122, the emperor gave up investing bishops with the ring and staff, the symbols of their spiritual office, and allowed church elections. In return he could attend elections and invest bishops with a sceptre for the lands they held from him. The dispute had weakened imperial authority and strengthened the German princes.

events.text: 'Holy' first used for the empire under Frederick I Barbarossa
events.detail: Frederick I, called Barbarossa ('Red Beard'), became emperor in 1155 and set out to restore imperial power, especially over the rich cities of northern Italy and in relation to the pope. In 1157 the word sacrum ('holy') first appeared in a document in connection with his empire. It expressed the idea that the empire was sacred in its own right, not dependent on the pope. The full form 'Holy Roman Empire' is recorded from 1254. Barbarossa spent much of his reign fighting in Italy, and he drowned in 1190 while on the Third Crusade.

events.text: Frederick II dies; Hohenstaufen power collapses, interregnum follows
events.detail: Frederick II of the Hohenstaufen dynasty ruled Germany, Italy and the Kingdom of Sicily. Constantly in conflict with the papacy, which lay hemmed in between his lands, he was excommunicated four times, and Pope Innocent IV declared him deposed in 1245. When Frederick died in December 1250, his son Conrad IV fought on, but died in 1254, and the Hohenstaufen collapsed. Rival kings were elected, some of them foreigners with little power in Germany. This period, often called the Great Interregnum, let the German princes take over much of the king's power and lands.

events.text: Rudolf of Habsburg elected King of the Romans
events.detail: After two decades without an effective king, the German princes wanted a ruler who could restore order but would not threaten their own power. In 1273 they elected Rudolf, Count of Habsburg, a minor noble from what is now Switzerland, as King of the Romans. Rudolf, who was never crowned emperor, defeated the powerful King Ottokar II of Bohemia and took Austria, Styria and Carinthia for his own family. This was the start of Habsburg power in the empire. From the 15th century almost every emperor was a Habsburg.

events.text: Charles IV's Golden Bull fixes the seven prince-electors
events.detail: Imperial elections had often led to disputes and rival kings. In 1356 Emperor Charles IV issued the Golden Bull at diets in Nuremberg and Metz. It named the seven prince-electors who would choose the king: the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier, the King of Bohemia, the Count Palatine of the Rhine, the Duke of Saxony and the Margrave of Brandenburg. It also set majority voting, with Frankfurt as the place of election. The Bull fixed the empire's constitution for more than four hundred years and strengthened the electors as near-independent rulers.

events.text: Diet of Worms launches the Imperial Reform
events.detail: By the late 15th century the empire was a patchwork of hundreds of territories with weak central institutions. In 1495 King Maximilian I asked the Diet (assembly) at Worms for taxes and troops for his wars against the Ottomans and France. The princes, led by the Archbishop of Mainz, agreed but demanded reforms in return. The Diet declared a Perpetual Public Peace banning private feuds and created an Imperial Chamber Court for the whole empire. It also agreed a general tax, the Common Penny, and these reforms gave the empire institutions that lasted until 1806.

events.text: Luther's break with the pope starts the Reformation
events.detail: In 1517 Martin Luther, a monk and professor at Wittenberg in Saxony, wrote his Ninety-five Theses against the sale of indulgences, certificates said to reduce punishment for sins. On 31 October he sent them to the Archbishop of Mainz, and they soon spread across Germany in print. His challenge to the pope's authority grew into the Protestant Reformation, and he was excommunicated in 1521. Many German princes and cities adopted Lutheranism, splitting the empire along religious lines. The division led to decades of conflict between Catholic emperors and Protestant princes.

events.text: Peace of Augsburg lets rulers choose Catholicism or Lutheranism
events.detail: After years of religious war in the empire, Emperor Charles V, through his brother Ferdinand, made peace with the Lutheran princes of the Schmalkaldic League. The Peace of Augsburg, signed on 25 September 1555, allowed each ruler to choose either Lutheranism or Catholicism as the official religion of his lands. This was later summed up as cuius regio, eius religio ('whose realm, his religion'). Calvinism was not included. The settlement made the religious division of the empire permanent and kept peace for over sixty years, until the Thirty Years' War.

events.text: Bohemian revolt starts the Thirty Years' War
events.detail: Bohemia had a large Protestant population and feared losing its religious freedoms under the Catholic Habsburgs. In 1618 Protestant nobles in Prague threw two imperial officials out of a castle window, the Defenestration of Prague, and rebelled. They replaced Ferdinand II as their king with the Protestant Frederick V of the Palatinate. The revolt grew into the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which drew in Denmark, Sweden, France and Spain. An estimated 4.5 to 8 million people died from fighting, famine and disease, and parts of Germany lost more than half their population.

events.text: Peace of Westphalia; Switzerland and the Dutch Republic leave
events.detail: The Thirty Years' War ended with two treaties signed in October 1648 at Münster and Osnabrück in Westphalia. Rulers could now choose Catholicism, Lutheranism or Calvinism. France gained lands in Alsace and Lorraine, and Sweden gained Western Pomerania and other territories on the Baltic and North Sea. The peace confirmed the legal independence of the Swiss Confederation, and the Dutch Republic, already recognised by Spain earlier that year, also left the empire. The empire survived, but its princes gained near-sovereign powers, and the emperor's authority was greatly weakened.

events.text: Franche-Comté lost to France
events.detail: Franche-Comté, the 'Free County' of Burgundy around Besançon, belonged to the Spanish Habsburgs but was part of the empire. King Louis XIV of France conquered it during his wars, and the Treaties of Nijmegen (1678–1679), which ended the Franco-Dutch War, gave France control of the region. It was the only noticeable change to the empire's outer borders between 1648 and 1806. On the map, the empire's western edge pulls back from the Jura mountains, and France now reached the Swiss border.

events.text: Francis II abdicates and dissolves the empire
events.detail: In 1804 Napoleon declared himself Emperor of the French, and Francis II responded by taking the extra title Emperor of Austria. After Austria's defeat at Austerlitz in December 1805, many of Francis's German vassals left the empire in July 1806 to form the Confederation of the Rhine under French protection. Fearing that Napoleon might claim the imperial title himself, Francis abdicated on 6 August 1806 and released all imperial states from their obligations. The Holy Roman Empire, which had lasted more than eight centuries, was dissolved and disappears from the map.

name: Great Seljuk Empire
summary: Oghuz Turks led by Tughril and Chaghri took Merv and Nishapur in 1037–38, crushed the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan and in 1055 entered Baghdad as protectors of the Abbasid caliph. Alp Arslan's victory at Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia, and under Malik-Shah and his vizier Nizam al-Mulk the empire stretched from the Levant to Central Asia. After 1092 it fragmented among rival heirs; Sanjar's defeat at Qatwan (1141) and capture by the Oghuz (1153) ended Seljuk power in the east, and the last sultan fell to the Khwarazmians in 1194, leaving only the Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia (to 1308).

events.text: Tughril and Chaghri take Merv and Nishapur (1037–38)
events.detail: The Seljuks were a family of Oghuz Turks, nomads from the steppes near the Aral Sea, named after their ancestor Seljuk. Driven out of Transoxiana in 1034, they moved with their herds into Khurasan, in north-eastern Iran, then ruled by the Ghaznavid Empire. Led by the brothers Tughril and Chaghri, they captured the great cities of Merv and Nishapur in 1037–1038, and in 1037 Tughril was proclaimed sultan. Historians date the Seljuk Empire from these conquests. For the first time the Turkmen nomads held major cities, and the empire appears on the map in Khurasan.

events.text: Seljuks rout the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan near Merv
events.detail: The Ghaznavid sultan Mas'ud, ruling from Ghazna in Afghanistan, marched with a large army to drive the Seljuks out of Khurasan. The Seljuks avoided open battle and harassed his columns with hit-and-run raids, so that his troops grew starving and demoralised. On 23 May 1040, around 16,000 Seljuk horsemen defeated the Ghaznavid army at Dandanaqan, near Merv. Mas'ud fled to India, where he was overthrown and later murdered. All of Khurasan passed to the Seljuks, who then turned west toward Iran.

events.text: Tughril enters Baghdad and ends Buyid influence
events.detail: After Dandanaqan, Tughril conquered much of Iran from the Buyids and made Isfahan his capital. The Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, al-Qa'im, was a figurehead under the Shia Buyid emirs, and he looked to the Sunni Seljuks for support. In 1055, invited by the caliph, Tughril entered Baghdad and ended Buyid rule there. The caliph recognised him as sultan, the ruler of the Muslim world's armies and government, while keeping religious authority himself. The Seljuk map now reached Iraq, and the Seljuks became protectors of Sunni Islam.

events.text: Alp Arslan adds Armenia and Georgia
events.detail: Alp Arslan, Chaghri's son, became sultan in 1063 after Tughril died. In 1064 he led a campaign into the Caucasus and besieged Ani, the old capital of Armenia, then held by the Byzantines. After a 25-day siege the Seljuk army took the city on 16 August 1064, and the caliph honoured him with the title 'Father of Conquests'. He also invaded Georgia, and King Gagik II of Kars became his vassal. The Seljuk frontier now pressed against Byzantine Anatolia.

events.text: Alp Arslan defeats and captures Romanos IV at Manzikert
events.detail: Turkmen raids into Byzantine Anatolia led Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes to march east with a large army. On 26 August 1071 he met Alp Arslan near Manzikert, north of Lake Van. Many of the emperor's mercenaries and levies fled, and Romanos himself was captured, the only Byzantine emperor ever taken prisoner by a Muslim commander. Alp Arslan released him in return for a ransom and a treaty. But Byzantium fell into civil war, and Turkish groups poured into central Anatolia, which they controlled as far as the Aegean within a few years.

events.text: Malik-Shah I succeeds; with Nizam al-Mulk, the golden age
events.detail: Alp Arslan was fatally wounded on a campaign in Central Asia in 1072, and his son Malik-Shah I succeeded him. Real power lay with the great Persian vizier Nizam al-Mulk, who had served his father and ran the government for twenty years. He founded the Nizamiyya madrasas, colleges across the empire, and is credited with a famous book on government. Under Malik-Shah the empire reached the height of its power, stretching from Anatolia and Syria to Central Asia. Isfahan, the capital, flourished.

events.text: Malik-Shah dies; the empire splits among his heirs
events.detail: In 1092 Nizam al-Mulk was assassinated near Baghdad by a man disguised as a Sufi (most accounts blame the Nizari Isma'ilis, or Assassins), and Malik-Shah died a few weeks later, on 19 November 1092, possibly poisoned. His brother and four sons then quarrelled over the throne, and the empire split. Syria broke into rival emirates such as Aleppo and Damascus, and in Anatolia the Sultanate of Rum and other Turkish states went their own way. On the map the empire still looks large, but in practice it was a loose collection of rival Seljuk princes and governors.

events.text: First Crusade takes Jerusalem; Crusader states carved out
events.detail: In 1095 Pope Urban II called for a crusade to help Byzantium against the Turks and to take Jerusalem. The divided Seljuk rulers of Syria and Anatolia were more interested in fighting one another, and they failed to stop the crusader armies, which took Nicaea, Antioch and other cities. Jerusalem had already been retaken from the Seljuks' vassals by the Fatimids of Egypt in 1098. On 15 July 1099 the crusaders stormed the city and massacred many of its people. They set up Crusader states along the coast of Syria and Palestine.

events.text: Ahmad Sanjar becomes sole sultan
events.detail: Ahmad Sanjar, a son of Malik-Shah, had governed Khurasan from his base at Merv since 1097. When his brother Sultan Muhammad I died in 1118, Sanjar defeated his young nephew Mahmud II and became supreme sultan, leaving Mahmud to rule western Iran and Iraq as his subordinate. He ruled for 41 years, mostly from Merv, and for much of that time he kept the borders of the empire largely intact. The Seljuk centre of power had moved east again, to Khurasan.

events.text: Qara Khitai crush Sanjar at Qatwan; eastern lands lost
events.detail: In Central Asia a new power arose: the Qara Khitai, refugees from the fallen Liao dynasty of northern China led by Yelü Dashi. Invited by the Khwarazmians, Sanjar's own vassals, and by Karluk Turks, they attacked the Seljuks' vassals. On 9 September 1141 they crushed Sanjar's army on the Qatwan steppe north of Samarkand, encircling it in a valley. Sanjar escaped, but his wife and many commanders were captured. The Seljuks lost all their lands beyond the Amu Darya up to the Syr Darya, and Khwarazm became a vassal of the Qara Khitai.

events.text: Oghuz tribes revolt and capture Sanjar
events.detail: Oghuz Turkmen tribes grazing near Balkh paid Sanjar a yearly tribute in sheep, but after quarrels with his officials, including the killing of a tax collector, the sultan marched against them. In April 1153 the Oghuz defeated and captured him. They held Sanjar prisoner for about three years, while they plundered the cities of Khurasan. The empire's eastern heartland was left in chaos. The defeat by the Seljuks' own kin is seen as the moment when the Great Seljuk Empire effectively collapsed.

events.text: Sanjar dies at Merv
events.detail: Sanjar escaped from his Oghuz captors in the autumn of 1156 and returned to Merv, but he died there on 8 May 1157. He was buried in a great domed tomb in Merv, and he was the last of the Great Seljuk sultans to rule the whole eastern empire. After his death Khurasan fell to local warlords and to the rising Khwarazmshahs, while the Seljuk sultans in western Iran became puppets of their own generals. On the map the empire shrinks to western Iran and Iraq.

events.text: Khwarazmshah Tekish defeats Toghrul III; the Great Seljuks end
events.detail: Tughril III became sultan in 1175, but power lay with the Eldiguzid atabegs, the commanders who ruled in his name. When Tughril tried to rule for himself, his rivals and the caliph al-Nasir called in the Khwarazmshah Tekish against him. In 1194 Tekish defeated and killed Tughril III near Rayy, and sent his head to the caliph in Baghdad. Tughril was the last Seljuk sultan of Iran. The Great Seljuk Empire ended, and its lands passed to the Khwarazmian Empire, while only the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum survived in Anatolia.
