name: Mongol Empire
summary: Proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206, Temüjin united the steppe and conquered northern China and the Khwarazmian Empire; his successors took the Jin, Rus' and the Abbasid caliphate, creating the largest contiguous land empire in history. After Möngke's death in 1259 the Toluid civil war split the empire into the Yuan dynasty and three western khanates (the Golden Horde, Chagatai Khanate and Ilkhanate). Kublai completed the conquest of Song China in 1279, but his attacks on Japan failed, and by his death in 1294 the four khanates went their own way.

events.text: Kurultai proclaims Temüjin Genghis Khan
events.detail: Temüjin was born around 1162, the son of a Mongol chieftain. After his father's death his family was abandoned and lived in poverty. Through skill in war and alliances, he defeated rival steppe leaders one by one, including his former allies Toghrul of the Kereits and Jamukha, and the Tatars, Merkits and Naimans. In 1206 an assembly of the steppe peoples, a kurultai, met near the Onon river and proclaimed him Genghis Khan, a title whose meaning is uncertain. For the first time the tribes of the Mongolian steppe were united under one ruler, and the Mongol Empire appears on the map.

events.text: Invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire begins (1219–1221)
events.detail: The Khwarazmian Empire ruled Central Asia and Iran under Shah Muhammad II. In 1218 Genghis Khan sent a large trading caravan there, but the governor of Otrar seized its goods and executed the merchants as spies. When the shah refused to punish him and killed one of the Mongol envoys sent to complain, Genghis invaded in 1219. Over the next two years Bukhara, Samarkand and Urgench fell, and the shah fled and died on an island in the Caspian Sea. The war was one of the bloodiest in history, and the empire's map now stretched west across Central Asia.

events.text: Genghis Khan dies during the campaign against Western Xia
events.detail: The Western Xia, a kingdom of the Tangut people in what is now north-western China, had submitted to the Mongols after a raid in 1209, but it later refused to send troops for the war against Khwarazm. Genghis Khan returned from the west to punish it. In August 1227, while subduing the rebellious Tanguts, he died, after falling from his horse while hunting the previous winter and growing increasingly ill. His burial place was kept secret and has never been found. The Western Xia was destroyed, and his son Ögedei was later chosen as Great Khan.

events.text: Mongols and Song finish off the Jin dynasty
events.detail: The Jin dynasty of the Jurchen people ruled northern China. The Mongols had attacked it since 1211, taking its capital Zhongdu (Beijing) in 1215 and forcing the Jin court to move south to Kaifeng. Under Ögedei the Mongols besieged Kaifeng in 1232, and the Jin emperor Aizong fled south to Caizhou. In 1233 the Southern Song dynasty allied with the Mongols, and their combined armies besieged Caizhou, which fell on 9 February 1234. The Jin dynasty ended, and the Mongols now ruled all of northern China, bringing them face to face with the Song.

events.text: Batu attacks Ryazan, the first Rus' principality to fall
events.detail: In 1236 a huge Mongol army under Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, with the general Subutai, set out to conquer the lands west of the Volga. In late 1237 it invaded Ryazan, the first of the Rus' principalities to be attacked, whose prince's call for help from Vladimir went unanswered. The Mongols besieged the city from 16 December, stormed it on 21 December, killed the prince and nearly all the inhabitants and burned it. Batu then pushed on into Vladimir-Suzdal, destroying city after city in the north-east of Rus'.

events.text: Kiev falls; nearly all Rus' under Mongol rule
events.detail: Kiev, the ancient capital of the Rus', had been the greatest city of Eastern Europe, though it was now weakened by quarrels among the princes. Batu's army, under the command of Subutai, besieged it from 28 November 1240 and stormed it on 6 December, after the defenders made a last stand in the Church of the Tithes. The fall of Kiev completed the conquest of the Rus' lands, which became tributaries of the Mongol khans, later known as the Golden Horde. The Mongol map now reached into Eastern Europe.

events.text: Hungarians crushed at Mohi; Ögedei's death halts the invasion
events.detail: In 1241 the Mongols invaded Central Europe. One force defeated the Poles and Germans at Legnica, while the main army under Batu and Subutai entered Hungary. On 11 April 1241 it destroyed the army of King Béla IV at Mohi, near the Sajó river, and went on to ravage Hungary. Then news arrived that the Great Khan Ögedei had died in December 1241, and the Mongol armies withdrew from Central Europe, though historians doubt this was the only reason. They never returned in such force.

events.text: Möngke elected Great Khan
events.detail: After Ögedei's death, his widow ruled as regent, then his son Güyük reigned briefly until his death in 1248. Batu, the most senior prince, backed Möngke, the son of Genghis Khan's youngest son Tolui. On 1 July 1251 a kurultai in Mongolia proclaimed Möngke Great Khan. He purged rival princes and reorganised the empire's government and finances. He then launched two great new campaigns: his brother Hulagu was sent west against the Islamic lands, and his brother Kublai south against the Song.

events.text: Hulagu sacks Baghdad and ends the Abbasid caliphate
events.detail: Hulagu destroyed the Isma'ili Assassins' strongholds in Iran and demanded that the Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim submit, but the caliph refused. The Mongols attacked Baghdad at the end of January 1258, and on 10 February the caliph surrendered. The city was sacked and its people massacred, and al-Musta'sim was killed. A later story says so many books were thrown into the Tigris that it ran black, though some libraries reopened within two years. The five-century Abbasid Caliphate of Baghdad was ended, and Iraq and Iran became the base of Hulagu's Ilkhanate.

events.text: Möngke dies besieging Diaoyu; succession war follows
events.detail: Möngke personally led an army against the Southern Song in Sichuan, where the Song had fortified mountain strongholds such as Diaoyu. In 1259 the Mongols besieged Diaoyu fortress, near modern Chongqing, but disease swept through their camp. Möngke died there on 11 August 1259, from disease according to most accounts, though one source says he was killed in battle. He had not named a successor, and his brothers Kublai and Ariq Böke fought each other in the Toluid Civil War (1260–1264). The empire began to break into separate khanates.

events.text: Mamluks defeat the Mongols at Ain Jalut
events.detail: Hulagu's army had taken Aleppo and Damascus and threatened Egypt, ruled by the Mamluks. After Möngke's death Hulagu withdrew with most of his army, leaving about 10,000 men under his general Kitbuqa. The Mamluk sultan Qutuz marched from Cairo, and on 3 September 1260 the two armies met at Ain Jalut, a spring in Galilee. Using a feigned retreat led by Baybars, the Mamluks defeated the Mongols and killed Kitbuqa. It was the first major halt to the Mongol advance, and Syria and Egypt stayed outside the empire.

events.text: Kublai proclaims the Yuan dynasty
events.detail: After winning the civil war, Kublai Khan ruled from northern China and adopted Chinese ways of government to win over his Chinese subjects. In 1271 he proclaimed a new dynasty with the Chinese name Dai Yuan, 'Great Yuan', and claimed succession to earlier Chinese dynasties. He built a new capital, Dadu (Khanbaliq), on the site of modern Beijing. As Great Khan he still had influence over the Ilkhanate and less over the Golden Horde. In practice, though, his real power was limited to the Yuan realm, which now became the core of the empire.

events.text: Song imperial court surrenders at Hangzhou
events.detail: Kublai's conquest of the Southern Song had stalled for years at Xiangyang, a fortress city on the Han river guarding the Yangtze plain. It fell in 1273, after the Mongols brought in Persian-designed counterweight trebuchets. The Mongol general Bayan then advanced down the Yangtze toward Hangzhou (Lin'an), the Song capital. In 1276 the Song court surrendered, and the boy emperor Gong was captured, while loyalists fled south with his younger brothers. Most of southern China was now in Mongol hands.

events.text: Conquest of Song China completed
events.detail: Song loyalists carried on the fight from southern China, crowning two young princes in turn. Their last refuge was a fleet at Yamen, in Guangdong near the Pearl River delta. On 19 March 1279 the Yuan navy under Zhang Hongfan destroyed the Song fleet. With the seven-year-old emperor Zhao Bing lost in the defeat, the Song dynasty ended, and Kublai became the first non-Han emperor to rule all of China. The Mongol Empire reached its greatest extent on the map around this time.

events.text: Second invasion of Japan fails, as the first did in 1274
events.detail: After the Korean kingdom of Goryeo submitted, Kublai demanded that Japan also become his vassal, but the Japanese ignored his envoys. In 1274 a Mongol and Korean force landed in Kyushu near Hakata but withdrew after a storm. The Japanese then built a defensive stone wall at Hakata Bay, and in 1281 Kublai sent a much larger invasion. It was held back by the samurai and then wrecked by a typhoon, which the Japanese called kamikaze, 'divine wind'. Japan stayed independent, and the failure marked one of the limits of Mongol expansion by sea.

name: Delhi Sultanate
summary: Founded in 1206 by Qutb ud-Din Aibak in the Indian lands of the Ghurids, the sultanate was ruled in turn by the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties. Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughluq pushed its armies deep into the south, briefly ruling most of the subcontinent, but rebellions created the Bahmani, Vijayanagara and other independent states. Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 left a small kingdom that the Lodis partly revived, until Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.

events.text: Iltutmish seizes the throne after Aibak's death
events.detail: The Delhi Sultanate grew out of the Indian conquests of Muhammad of Ghor, whose Turkic slave-commander Qutb ud-Din Aibak ruled the Ghurid lands in India after 1206. Iltutmish had been sold into slavery as a boy and bought by Aibak, rising to govern Badaun. When Aibak died, Iltutmish overthrew his unpopular successor Aram Shah in 1211 and made Delhi his capital. India's former Ghurid lands were then split among rival commanders. Iltutmish spent the next years fighting them and bringing rebel Hindu chiefs back under Delhi's control.

events.text: Iltutmish annexes much of Punjab and Sindh
events.detail: Since Aibak's death, Sindh and much of Punjab had been held by Nasir ad-Din Qabacha, another former Ghurid slave, based at Uch and Multan. In the early 1220s the Indus valley was fought over by Qabacha, Khwarazmian refugees and the Mongols, and Iltutmish kept out. In 1228 he invaded, defeated Qabacha and annexed large parts of Punjab and Sindh. Soon after, the Abbasid caliph recognised his authority in India. The Sultanate on the map now stretched from the Indus to Bengal.

events.text: Razia becomes sultan, one of few female rulers in Islamic history
events.detail: Iltutmish had chosen his daughter Razia as heir, saying she was more capable than his sons. But when he died in 1236 the nobles put her half-brother Ruknuddin Firuz on the throne. During a rebellion against him and his mother, Razia won over the people of Delhi and took power in 1236. The first female Muslim ruler of the Indian subcontinent, she disappointed the Turkic nobles, who had expected a figurehead, by ruling in her own right and promoting non-Turkic officers. They deposed her in 1240, and she was killed soon after.

events.text: Balban takes power and breaks the 'Forty'
events.detail: Balban had been a slave and one of the 'Forty', the powerful group of Turkic nobles at the Delhi court. After twenty years as chief minister to Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud, on Mahmud's death in 1266 Balban took the throne himself. Determined to restore the crown's authority, he broke up the Forty, set spies on his officials and insisted that the sultan was the 'shadow of God', requiring courtiers to prostrate themselves before him. He crushed rebels in Mewat and Bengal and held off the Mongols, keeping the Sultanate together.

events.text: Khalji revolution ends the Mamluk dynasty
events.detail: After Balban's death in 1287, his grandson Qaiqabad proved a weak ruler and was paralysed by illness. Nobles placed his infant son Kayumars on the throne and tried to kill Jalal-ud-Din Khalji, a senior commander. In 1290 Jalal-ud-Din deposed Kayumars and made himself sultan. His Khalji clan was of Turkic origin but had long lived in Afghanistan, and the old Turkic nobility saw them as outsiders. The 'Khalji revolution' ended the rule of the slave sultans, often called the Mamluk dynasty, and opened power to a wider group of nobles.

events.text: Alauddin Khalji's armies invade Gujarat (annexed 1304)
events.detail: Alauddin Khalji seized the throne in 1296 by murdering his uncle Jalal-ud-Din, and he set out to conquer the rich kingdoms beyond the Sultanate. Gujarat, in western India, was a wealthy trading region ruled by the Vaghela king Karna. In 1299 Alauddin's generals Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan raided it and sacked its cities. It was finally annexed in 1304. Gujarat's ports and wealth now belonged to Delhi, and the map pushed west to the Arabian Sea.

events.text: Chittor captured; a major Mongol invasion of Delhi is repelled
events.detail: Chittor, in Mewar, was a great hill fortress ruled by the Guhila king Ratnasimha. Alauddin set out in January 1303 and took it in August after a siege of nearly eight months. Later legends, especially the poem Padmavat, say he wanted Ratnasimha's beautiful queen Padmini, but most historians reject this story. While Alauddin was away, a Mongol army from the Chagatai Khanate under Taraghai invaded and besieged Delhi for over two months. Alauddin held out in a fortified camp at Siri until the Mongols withdrew, and he then strengthened his frontier defences.

events.text: Malik Kafur's campaign sacks Madurai in the far south
events.detail: Alauddin's slave-general Malik Kafur led a series of campaigns south of the Vindhya mountains, against kingdoms that had never been ruled from Delhi. After forcing the rulers of Devagiri (1308) and Warangal (1310) to pay tribute, he set out in October 1310 for the far south. In 1311 he besieged the Hoysala capital, Dwarasamudra, and then raided the Pandya kingdom of Madurai, reaching almost to the southern tip of India. He returned with enormous treasure, elephants and horses. These were mostly raids, but they made Delhi the dominant power across the peninsula.

events.text: Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq founds the Tughlaq dynasty
events.detail: After Alauddin's death in 1316, the Khalji dynasty collapsed amid murders and plots, and in 1320 the throne was seized by Khusrau Khan. Ghazi Malik, a veteran commander who had fought the Mongols on the north-western frontier, rose against him, defeated him and became sultan as Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq. He founded the Tughlaq dynasty and built the fortress city of Tughlaqabad near Delhi. His armies brought Warangal under direct rule in 1323. He died in 1325 when a pavilion built in his honour collapsed.

events.text: Muhammad bin Tughluq moves the capital to Daulatabad
events.detail: Muhammad bin Tughluq ruled one of the largest areas of any Delhi sultan, reaching down to Madurai in the far south. In 1327 he ordered the capital moved from Delhi to Devagiri in the Deccan, which he renamed Daulatabad. It lay in a more central position for ruling both north and south, and Ibn Battuta says it was safer from Mongol attack. He even summoned nobles, officials and scholars to move there, causing great hardship. Soon after, revolts broke out in Madurai (1334), Bengal and elsewhere, and the empire began to shrink.

events.text: Bahmani Sultanate breaks away in the Deccan
events.detail: As revolts against Muhammad bin Tughluq's harsh rule spread in the 1340s, rebel officers in the Deccan rose against Delhi in 1347. Their first leader, Ismail Mukh, stepped aside for Zafar Khan, founder of the Bahmani Sultanate with its capital at Gulbarga. Delhi lost its lands south of the Vindhyas, and the Bahmanis went on to fight the Hindu Vijayanagara Empire to the south. On the map the Sultanate retreats to northern India.

events.text: Timur sacks Delhi
events.detail: By the 1390s the Tughlaq dynasty was in decline, split by rival claimants to the throne. In 1398 Timur, the Turko-Mongol conqueror from Samarkand, invaded India and on 17 December defeated the army of Sultan Mahmud Shah II outside the city. Delhi, then one of the richest cities in the world, was sacked and left in ruins. Estimates of those killed range from 100,000 to 200,000. The Sultanate never recovered its former power, as provincial governors broke away.

events.text: Khizr Khan founds the Sayyid dynasty
events.detail: Khizr Khan had been governor of Multan and had dealt with Timur as an envoy and negotiator during his invasion. In 1414 he took Delhi and founded the Sayyid dynasty, which claimed descent from the Prophet, though historians doubt the claim. Afraid of offending Timur's successors, he never took a royal title and ruled with modest titles instead. The Sayyids controlled only a small area around Delhi and constantly fought rebellious governors. On the map the Sultanate is at its smallest in this period.

events.text: Bahlul Lodi founds the Lodi dynasty
events.detail: Bahlul Lodi was the chief of an Afghan tribe who governed Sirhind in Punjab. The last Sayyid ruler, Alam Shah, withdrew to Badaun, and in 1451 he abdicated in Bahlul's favour. Bahlul became the first Afghan sultan of Delhi and founded the Lodi dynasty. He crushed rebellions and in 1479 defeated and annexed the Jaunpur Sultanate to the east. Under the Lodis the Sultanate grew again across the Ganges plain, and the map expands to cover much of northern India.

events.text: Babur defeats and kills Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat
events.detail: Ibrahim Lodi, sultan from 1517, quarrelled with his relatives and nobles. Daulat Khan Lodi, the governor of Punjab, invited Babur, a Timurid prince ruling Kabul, to invade. On 21 April 1526, at Panipat north of Delhi, Babur's army defeated Ibrahim's forces, using field cannon and firearms, among the first in India. Ibrahim was killed in the battle. The Delhi Sultanate came to an end, and Babur founded the Mughal Empire, which ruled most of the subcontinent for the next two centuries.

name: Mali Empire
summary: Sundiata Keita's victory over the Sosso at Kirina (c. 1235) founded the Mali Empire, which absorbed old Ghana and controlled the gold and salt trade of the western Sahel. It peaked in the 14th century under Mansa Musa, whose 1324 pilgrimage through Cairo became legendary, and Sulayman, whose court Ibn Battuta visited. After 1360 weak rulers, Tuareg and Mossi raids and the rise of Songhai cost it Timbuktu, Gao and the north; a last attempt to take Djenné failed in 1599 and the empire broke up after Mahmud IV's death c. 1610.

events.text: c. 1240: Sundiata takes the old Ghana capital
events.detail: Mali grew from small Mandinka kingdoms on the upper Niger that had once been vassals of the Ghana Empire. When the Sosso king Soumaoro Kanté conquered much of the region, the exiled prince Sundiata Keita returned and led an alliance of Mandinka and other states that defeated the Sosso at Kirina in about 1235. According to the World History Encyclopedia, Sundiata then captured the old Ghana capital in 1240. Ghana's lands, with their trade routes and gold, became part of Mali. Mali replaced Ghana as the great power of the western Sahel.

events.text: c. 1255: Sundiata dies; his son Uli succeeds
events.detail: Sundiata is remembered as Mali's founder and the hero of the Mandinka epic that bears his name. He was the first ruler to take the title mansa, meaning king or emperor, and his capital was at Niani. When he died, around 1255, he was succeeded by his son, called Uli in oral tradition and Wali in Arabic sources. Like later mansas, Uli made the pilgrimage to Mecca, showing the dynasty's links to the wider Muslim world.

events.text: General Sakura, a former slave, seizes the throne
events.detail: After Uli's reign, Mali went through a period of political instability among the Keita princes. Around 1285 (an estimate by the French scholar Delafosse), Sakura, who was not a member of the Keita family and may once have been a slave of the royal court, seized the throne. He was a successful general and led Mali to considerable expansion, west toward the Atlantic and east beyond Gao, according to Ibn Khaldun. He was killed in the early 1300s while returning from the pilgrimage to Mecca, and the Keita dynasty was restored.

events.text: c. 1312: Musa becomes mansa
events.detail: Musa became mansa around 1312. According to his own account, his predecessor had sailed west into the Atlantic with a great fleet and never returned, leaving Musa as his deputy in charge. Some historians suspect Musa simply deposed him and invented the story. At his accession Mali already covered much of the former Ghana Empire. Musa went on to make Mali richer and larger than ever, and he became the best-known ruler in its history.

events.text: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage passes through Cairo with lavish gold
events.detail: Mali was probably the largest gold producer in the world, and much of the gold used around the Mediterranean came from West Africa. In 1324 Musa made the pilgrimage to Mecca with a huge caravan and a vast supply of gold. In Cairo his lavish gifts were said to have noticeably lowered the value of gold in Egypt. Officials he met there passed information about Mali to Arab historians such as al-Umari. The journey made Musa famous across the Muslim world and Europe, and Mali appeared on later European maps, such as the Catalan Atlas.

events.text: c. 1325: Musa, back from Mecca, builds mosques and palaces in Timbuktu
events.detail: According to the Tarikh al-Sudan, Gao and Timbuktu submitted to Musa as he travelled home from Mecca, although modern historians doubt this account, and Gao may already have been taken by his general. What is clearer is that Musa brought scholars and architects back with him, including the Andalusian poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili. He built mosques and palaces in Timbuktu, including part of the Djinguereber Mosque. Timbuktu grew into a famous centre of Islamic learning. With the Niger Bend cities in Mali's hands, the empire reached its greatest extent on the map.

events.text: Ibn Battuta visits the court of Mansa Sulayman (1352–53)
events.detail: Musa's son Maghan I was deposed in 1341 by his uncle Sulayman, who ruled for 19 years. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visited Mali and stayed at Sulayman's court from 1352 to 1353. He wrote the first eyewitness account of a West African kingdom, describing the court ceremonies of Mansa Sulayman and praising the safety of the empire and its people's 'lack of oppression'. His account shows Mali at the height of its wealth and power.

events.text: Sulayman dies, ending Mali's golden age
events.detail: Sulayman died in 1360. His death marked the end of Mali's golden age, as quarrels over the succession among the Keita princes weakened the empire. In the following decades rival claimants and powerful officials struggled for control of the throne. Meanwhile pressure grew on the empire's northern frontier, where Tuareg Berbers from the Sahara fought Mali's forces and in the 1370s devastated the city of Gao. Mali stayed large on the map for some time, but its grip on its outer provinces began to slip.

events.text: Timbuktu lost to the Tuareg (1433–34)
events.detail: Timbuktu, on the Niger Bend, was Mali's great trading and learning centre where the Saharan caravan routes met the river. In 1433–1434 Mali lost control of the city to the Tuareg, led by Akil Ag-Amalwal. The Tuareg held it until the Songhai ruler Sonni Ali captured it in 1468. The loss cut Mali off from the main trans-Saharan trade route. Its northern frontier now pulled back from the desert edge, and the map shows the empire shrinking toward the south and west.

events.text: Songhai conquers Mema, one of Mali's oldest provinces
events.detail: Songhai, centred at Gao on the middle Niger, had once been a vassal of Mali but became independent and expanded rapidly under Sonni Ali. In 1465 Songhai conquered Mema, one of Mali's oldest possessions, whose king had sheltered the young Sundiata in exile. Songhai was now Mali's main rival, and within a few years it would take Timbuktu as well. On the map the Niger Bend passes from Mali to Songhai, and Mali's eastern lands begin to fall away.

events.text: Mossi raiders conquer Macina
events.detail: Mali's grip on its northern provinces was weakening, and the Mossi kingdoms to the south had been raiding the Macina region on the inner Niger Delta. In 1477 the Mossi emperor Naba Nasséré launched another raid into Macina, this time conquering it and the old province of BaGhana (Wagadu), Ghana's former heartland. Mali lost more of its northern territory. The empire was being squeezed between Songhai to the east and the Mossi to the south.

events.text: Mansa Mahmud II receives Portuguese envoys
events.detail: Portuguese ships had been trading along the West African coast since the mid-15th century. Their traders found that the peoples of the Gambia river region were still subjects of the mansa of Mali. Hoping to stop Mali's decline, Mansa Mahmud II opened diplomatic relations with Portugal, receiving the envoys Pêro d'Évora and Gonçalo Enes in 1487. The contact shows that Mali still controlled western lands near the Atlantic coast. Its future increasingly lay there, while Songhai dominated the Niger Bend.

events.text: Askia Muhammad I of Songhai seizes the province of Diafunu
events.detail: Under Askia Muhammad I, the Songhai Empire continued to expand westward at Mali's expense. In 1502 Songhai forces defeated the Malian general Fati Quali Keita and seized the province of Diafunu. Later, in 1544 or 1545, a Songhai army even sacked Mali's capital. Mali was now a regional power confined to the upper Niger and the lands toward the Gambia and Senegal rivers. On the map it is a much smaller kingdom.

events.text: Mali army defeated outside Djenné by Moroccan troops
events.detail: After Morocco invaded and destroyed the Songhai Empire in the 1590s, Mali tried to win back power along the Niger. Mansa Mahmud IV gathered allies and marched on Djenné, but the governor of Kala, Bukar, secretly went over to the Moroccans. On 26 April 1599 the Moroccan musketeers, helped by Bukar's support, defeated the Malian army outside Djenné, though Mahmud escaped. According to the Mali Empire article, this defeat marked the end of the empire. Mali's hopes of revival were over.

events.text: c. 1610: Mahmud IV dies and the empire breaks up
events.detail: Mahmud IV died around 1610. According to oral tradition, his three sons fought over what remained of Manden, the Mandinka heartland. The kingdom broke up into small rival states, and the Keita family retreated to the town of Kangaba, on the upper Niger, where they lived on as provincial chiefs, holding only a small part of the former empire. The Mali Empire, which had once stretched from the Atlantic to beyond the Niger Bend, disappears from the map.

name: Aztec Empire
summary: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, traditionally in 1325, and served the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco until they overthrew them in 1428 and formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan. Under Itzcoatl, Moctezuma I, Axayacatl and Ahuitzotl the alliance built a tributary empire across central Mexico to the Gulf, Oaxaca and Soconusco, though it was halted by the Purépecha in the west. Cortés arrived in 1519 with Indigenous allies; after smallpox and a long siege, Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521, after the map ends.

events.text: c. 1375: Acamapichtli becomes the first tlatoani of Tenochtitlan
events.detail: The Mexica had settled on an island in Lake Texcoco, in the Valley of Mexico, where they founded Tenochtitlan, traditionally in 1325. It was a small city paying tribute to the powerful Tepanec city of Azcapotzalco. After the death of their leader Tenoch, the elders chose a king with prestigious connections: Acamapichtli, a noble from Culhuacan whose rulers claimed descent from the ancient Toltecs. He became the first tlatoani (king) of Tenochtitlan and founded its royal dynasty. The chronicles disagree on his dates, placing the start of his reign between 1350 and 1376.

events.text: Tenochtitlan and allies defeat Azcapotzalco; Triple Alliance formed
events.detail: For decades Tenochtitlan fought as a junior ally of Azcapotzalco, helping it build a tributary empire. When the Tepanec king Tezozomoc died in 1426, his son Maxtla seized power, turned on the Mexica and blockaded their city, and their king Chimalpopoca died, possibly murdered. The new Mexica king Itzcoatl allied with Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco, the city of Tlacopan and Huexotzinco. Together they defeated Azcapotzalco in 1428. Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan formed the Triple Alliance, and the Aztec Empire begins on the map.

events.text: Moctezuma I succeeds Itzcoatl; expansion to the Gulf and Oaxaca
events.detail: Moctezuma I, a nephew of Itzcoatl, had been one of his leading generals and was chosen as ruler on Itzcoatl's death in 1440. Early in his reign he conquered Oaxaca, and he went on to push the empire beyond the Valley of Mexico to the Gulf Coast for the first time, subduing the Huastec and Totonac peoples. This brought luxury goods such as cacao, rubber, cotton and feathers to Tenochtitlan as tribute. He also faced frost, drought and severe famine in the 1450s. By his death in 1469, the empire stretched from the Gulf toward the Pacific.

events.text: Axayacatl retakes the Toluca Valley from the Purépecha
events.detail: The Toluca Valley, west of the Valley of Mexico, was home to the Matlatzinca people and lay on the frontier with the Purépecha (Tarascan) Empire of Michoacán, the Aztecs' great western rival. According to the Aztec Empire article, the Purépecha had invaded the valley in 1455. Axayacatl, Moctezuma I's successor, retook it in 1472 and held it against Purépecha counterattacks. The article on Axayacatl dates his Toluca campaign to 1474. The valley became the Aztecs' heavily defended western frontier.

events.text: Aztec invasion of the Purépecha Empire ends in heavy defeat
events.detail: Encouraged by his success in the Toluca Valley, Axayacatl launched a major invasion of the Purépecha Empire. According to the Aztec Empire article, in 1479 he led 32,000 soldiers into Michoacán and met a Purépecha army of 50,000 just across the border, which killed or captured over 90% of his force. The article on Axayacatl dates the defeat to 1476. Axayacatl was wounded and never fought the Purépecha again. It was the Aztecs' first major defeat, and the Purépecha frontier, fortified afterwards, permanently blocked Aztec expansion to the west.

events.text: Ahuitzotl takes power; conquests reach Oaxaca and Soconusco
events.detail: After Axayacatl's brother Tizoc died, probably murdered by his own nobles, another brother, Ahuitzotl, took power in 1486. He first crushed rebellions, then launched a great wave of conquests. His armies took the Oaxaca Valley, conquered Mixtec and Zapotec peoples and pushed down the Pacific coast as far as Soconusco, near today's border with Guatemala. He also rebuilt the Templo Mayor, the great temple of Tenochtitlan, on a grander scale in 1487. Under Ahuitzotl the Aztec Empire reached close to its greatest extent on the map.

events.text: Moctezuma II succeeds Ahuitzotl
events.detail: When Ahuitzotl died in 1502, his nephew Moctezuma II, son of Axayacatl, was chosen as ruler. He set out to centralise power, creating new provinces and replacing many of his predecessors' advisers. He also widened the gap between nobles and commoners, barring commoners from serving in the royal palace or high office. He continued campaigns of conquest early in his reign and fought 'flower wars' against Tlaxcala, the Aztecs' unconquered enemy to the east. The empire was at its height, but many subject peoples resented its heavy tribute.

events.text: Aztec armies invade the Purépecha Empire again
events.detail: The Purépecha Empire to the west remained undefeated since Axayacatl's disaster decades earlier, and border clashes continued. In 1515 Aztec armies commanded by the Tlaxcalan general Tlahuicole invaded Purépecha territory again. They failed to take any land and were mostly limited to raiding, and the Purépecha defeated them and forced them to withdraw. The western frontier stayed where it was. Just four years later, Spanish ships would appear on the Gulf coast.

events.text: Cortés lands and founds Veracruz; enters Tenochtitlan in November
events.detail: In 1519 the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés sailed from Cuba with a small expedition. In April he landed on the Gulf coast, where he founded the settlement of Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz and allied with the Totonac city of Cempoala. With the help of his interpreter, La Malinche, he gathered indigenous allies, above all the Tlaxcalans, who were the Aztecs' bitter enemies. On 8 November 1519 he entered Tenochtitlan and met Moctezuma II. Soon afterwards he took the emperor captive in his own city.

events.text: Moctezuma dies; Spaniards flee on La Noche Triste; smallpox spreads
events.detail: In May 1520 the Spaniard Pedro de Alvarado massacred Aztec nobles during the festival of Toxcatl, and the city rose against the Spaniards. In late June Moctezuma died in unclear circumstances, perhaps killed by the Spaniards, perhaps by his own people. On 30 June, La Noche Triste ('the Sad Night'), the Spaniards and Tlaxcalans fled Tenochtitlan with heavy losses. A smallpox epidemic then swept the city, killing the new ruler Cuitlahuac in December. Weakened by disease, Tenochtitlan fell to Cortés and his allies in August 1521.

name: Timurid Empire
summary: Timur took control of the western Chagatai lands around 1370 (the map starts in 1375) and in three decades of campaigns conquered Iran and Iraq, broke the Golden Horde, sacked Delhi, Damascus and Baghdad and defeated the Ottomans at Ankara. After his death in 1405 his son Shah Rukh ruled from Herat over a smaller realm that saw the Timurid Renaissance. Civil wars, the Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu cost the dynasty western Iran, and the Uzbeks took Samarkand (1501) and Herat (1507); Babur, a Timurid, went on to found the Mughal Empire.

events.text: Timur takes Isfahan, massacring the city after it revolts
events.detail: Timur, a Turco-Mongol warlord from Transoxiana, had made himself master of the western Chagatai Khanate by 1370. After the collapse of the Ilkhanate, Persia was split among rival dynasties, and from 1383 Timur set out to conquer them. When he reached Isfahan in 1387, the city surrendered and was at first treated mercifully, but its people then rose up and killed his tax collectors and soldiers, and Timur ordered a massacre. The death toll is reckoned at 100,000 to 200,000, and an eyewitness counted towers of skulls. Central Persia now came under Timur's rule.

events.text: Kartid rulers removed from Herat
events.detail: The Kartid dynasty ruled Herat, a great city of Khurasan in western Afghanistan. Timur began his Persian campaign there, and when Herat refused to surrender he reduced it to rubble and massacred most of its people. The Kartid rulers then became his vassals. In 1389, less than a decade later, Timur's son Miran Shah removed them and annexed their kingdom outright. Herat was now firmly part of Timur's empire, and in the next century it became one of its two great capitals, alongside Samarkand.

events.text: Timur captures Shiraz and seizes Baghdad
events.detail: In 1393 Timur turned to southern Persia and Iraq. Shiraz, the capital of the Muzaffarid dynasty, surrendered, and when the Muzaffarid prince Shah Mansur rebelled he was defeated and the dynasty was annexed. In August the same year Timur took Baghdad by surprise, marching there from Shiraz in only eight days. Its Jalayirid ruler, Sultan Ahmad, fled to Syria, where the Mamluk sultan Barquq sheltered him. Timur's empire now reached across Iraq to the edge of Mamluk Syria.

events.text: Timur crushes Tokhtamysh's Golden Horde (1394–95)
events.detail: Tokhtamysh had become khan of the Golden Horde with Timur's help, but he turned against his former patron and invaded Timur's lands from 1385. After years of fighting, Timur launched a final assault in 1395 and routed Tokhtamysh at the Battle of the Terek River on 15 April. He then destroyed the Golden Horde's major cities, including its capital Sarai, Astrakhan and the Italian trading posts at Tana. The Golden Horde never recovered its former power. Timur did not keep the steppe lands, but he had broken his most dangerous rival in the north.

events.text: Timur invades India and sacks Delhi
events.detail: The Delhi Sultanate was weakened by quarrels within the Tughlaq dynasty. In 1398 Timur invaded India, crossing the Indus on 30 September with an army reported at 90,000. On 17 December 1398 he defeated the army of Sultan Mahmud Shah II outside Delhi. The city, one of the richest in the world, was sacked and reduced to ruins, and Timur soon returned to Samarkand with enormous plunder. He did not try to hold India, which stayed outside his empire on the map.

events.text: Damascus taken; Baghdad destroyed
events.detail: In 1399 Timur went to war with the Mamluk sultan of Egypt and the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I. In 1400 he invaded Armenia and Georgia, then turned to Syria and sacked Aleppo and Damascus, where he met the historian Ibn Khaldun in 1401. In June 1401 he attacked Baghdad, which had been retaken by its former rulers, and destroyed the city and massacred its people. Timur's armies now dominated the whole region from Syria to India, though he did not try to rule Syria directly.

events.text: Timur defeats and captures the Ottoman sultan at Ankara
events.detail: Timur and the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I were the two great powers of the Muslim world, and they quarrelled over vassals in eastern Anatolia. In 1402 Bayezid broke off his blockade of Constantinople to meet Timur. When the armies met on the Çubuk plain near Ankara on 28 July 1402, Timur's army of about 140,000 defeated Bayezid's smaller force, as the Black Tatars and Anatolian troops deserted Bayezid and joined Timur. Bayezid was captured, the only Ottoman sultan ever taken in battle, and he died in captivity. The Ottoman state fell into a decade of civil war.

events.text: Timur dies at Farab (Otrar) on his way to invade China
events.detail: After his western victories Timur returned to Samarkand and prepared to invade Ming China. In December 1404 he set out east with a large army, despite the winter. He fell ill while camped beyond the Syr Darya and died at Farab, near Otrar, on 17 or 18 February 1405, before reaching the Chinese border. He was buried in the Gur-e-Amir in Samarkand. His sons and grandsons soon began fighting over his vast empire, and its western lands began to fall away.

events.text: Shah Rukh dies; the Qara Qoyunlu drive Timurids out of western Iran
events.detail: Timur's son Shah Rukh emerged victorious from the struggle for succession and ruled from 1405 to 1447, moving the capital to Herat. His reign was a golden age of art and learning, the 'Timurid Renaissance'. When he died in March 1447, his empire lost its strong central ruler. The Qara Qoyunlu, a Turkmen confederation from Azerbaijan under Jahan Shah, drove the Timurids out of western Iran and later even briefly occupied Herat in 1458. The map shrinks sharply in the west.

events.text: Ulugh Beg executed after his son's revolt; civil war follows
events.detail: Ulugh Beg, Shah Rukh's son, had governed Samarkand for decades and was a famous astronomer and mathematician, who built a great observatory and a madrasa there. He became ruler on his father's death in 1447, but he was a poor politician and could not control his relatives. His own son, Abd al-Latif, revolted, and in October 1449 Ulugh Beg was overthrown and killed. His death plunged the Timurid realm into civil war among rival princes. The empire was soon divided among competing branches of the family.

events.text: Abu Sa'id killed by Uzun Hasan; Persia lost for good
events.detail: Abu Sa'id Mirza, a great-grandson of Timur, reunited much of the empire in the 1450s, taking Herat in 1457. After the Qara Qoyunlu leader Jahan Shah was killed in 1467 by Uzun Hasan of the rival Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen, Abu Sa'id marched west to claim western Iran. In early 1469 Uzun Hasan defeated and captured him and handed him to a rival Timurid prince, who had him executed. The Timurids lost Persia permanently to the Aq Qoyunlu, and the empire was divided for good.

events.text: Uzbeks under Shaybani Khan take Samarkand
events.detail: After 1469 the Timurid lands were split between rival princes in Transoxiana and Herat. The Uzbeks, nomads from the steppe north of the Syr Darya, were led by Muhammad Shaybani, a former soldier in Timurid service. He drove the Timurids from Samarkand in 1500. The young Timurid prince Babur briefly retook the city, but in 1501 Shaybani captured it again and took Bukhara, founding the Shaybanid dynasty. Transoxiana, the Timurids' homeland, was lost, and Babur was forced to seek a new kingdom further south.

events.text: Herat falls to the Uzbeks; main Timurid rule ends
events.detail: Herat, ruled from 1469 by Husayn Bayqara, had become the last great centre of Timurid culture, home to artists and poets. Husayn Bayqara died in May 1506, and his sons were unable to resist the Uzbeks. In 1507 Muhammad Shaybani captured Herat, conquering almost all the surviving Timurid principalities. The main line of Timurid rule ended. One Timurid prince, Babur, survived in Kabul, and in 1526 he invaded India and founded the Mughal Empire.

name: Inca Empire
summary: After defeating the Chanka, Pachacuti (traditionally from 1438) turned the kingdom of Cusco into Tawantinsuyu, and he and his son Topa Inca conquered the Andes from Ecuador to central Chile, including the coastal kingdom of Chimor. At its height under Huayna Capac it was the largest empire in pre-Columbian America. Disease and a succession war between Huáscar and Atahualpa weakened it just as Pizarro arrived; Atahualpa was seized at Cajamarca in 1532 and executed in 1533, though Inca resistance continued at Vilcabamba until 1572.

events.text: c. 1470: The Incas conquer Chimor and its capital Chan Chan
events.detail: Chimor, the kingdom of the Chimú people, ruled the desert coast of northern Peru from its great capital, Chan Chan. Its people farmed irrigated river valleys and were famed for their pottery and fine work in gold, silver and copper. It was the last kingdom with any chance of stopping the Incas. Around 1470 the Inca prince Topa Inca Yupanqui, commanding for his father Pachacuti, defeated the Chimú ruler Minchançaman. Skilled Chimú artists were later brought to Cusco to work for the Inca rulers, and the Inca map now stretched along the northern coast of Peru.

events.text: Topa Inca Yupanqui succeeds Pachacuti and doubles the empire
events.detail: Pachacuti had turned the small kingdom of Cusco into Tawantinsuyu, the 'land of four parts', and with his son Topa Inca brought much of Peru under Inca rule. When Pachacuti died in 1471, Topa Inca became Sapa Inca, or sole ruler, and reigned until 1493. He extended the empire north along the Andes through modern Ecuador, rebuilding Quito. In the south he pushed into what is now Chile, toward the Maule river, where the Mapuche resisted. Under him the empire roughly doubled in size, and it became the largest state in the pre-Columbian Americas.

events.text: Huayna Capac succeeds and extends Inca rule into Ecuador
events.detail: Topa Inca died around 1493, and after a struggle over the succession his son Huayna Capac became Sapa Inca. He continued the empire's expansion. In the south he pushed further into what is now Chile and Argentina. In the north he campaigned through Ecuador into southern Colombia, and he became so attached to Ecuador that he spent most of his reign there, ruling from Tumebamba (Cuenca) and Quito. Under him the Inca Empire reached its greatest extent, stretching some 3,500 km from north to south.

events.text: Push into the Amazon near the Chinchipe is stopped by the Shuar
events.detail: From their highland base, the Incas also tried to expand east into the lowland forests of the Amazon basin, but these lands were very different from the Andean valleys they knew. In Ecuador, Huayna Capac's forces pushed into the Amazon lowlands as far as the Chinchipe river. There they were stopped and pushed back by the Shuar, a forest people of the eastern lowlands. The Inca Empire article dates this setback to 1527. It marked the eastern limit of Inca expansion in the north.

events.text: c. 1527: Huayna Capac dies, possibly of a European disease
events.detail: Huayna Capac died around 1527, after returning from campaigns in the far north with a fever. He may have died of a European disease such as smallpox or measles, which spread ahead of the Spaniards who had reached the Pacific coast, although some historians dispute this. His chosen heir, Ninan Cuyochi, died at about the same time. The deaths left no clear successor. Two of Huayna Capac's sons, Huáscar in Cusco and Atahualpa in the north, both claimed the throne.

events.text: Atahualpa defeats his brother Huáscar in the civil war
events.detail: Huáscar, crowned in Cusco, began a war against his half-brother Atahualpa, who commanded the veteran armies stationed in the north. The Inca Civil War lasted from 1529 to 1532 and devastated the empire. Atahualpa's generals Chalcuchimac and Quizquiz won a series of victories, and in 1532 they routed Huáscar's last army near Cusco and captured him. Atahualpa was now master of the empire. But the war had left it divided and exhausted just as a small band of Spaniards arrived.

events.text: Pizarro seizes Atahualpa at Cajamarca (16 November)
events.detail: Francisco Pizarro, a Spanish conquistador, had landed in Peru with a small force of about 168 men. Atahualpa, camped near Cajamarca with a large army, agreed to meet him. On 16 November 1532 he entered the town's plaza with thousands of attendants, mostly unarmed. After the friar Vicente de Valverde demanded that he accept Christianity and the Spanish king, the hidden Spaniards attacked with guns, cannon and horses. They killed thousands and captured Atahualpa, leaving the empire without its ruler.

events.text: Atahualpa executed; Spaniards take Cusco in November
events.detail: In captivity Atahualpa offered a huge ransom of gold and silver for his release, and he arranged for his captive brother Huáscar to be killed. After the Spaniards had collected the ransom, they accused him of treason and of murdering Huáscar. He was baptised and then executed by garrotte, on 29 August 1533 according to most accounts. Pizarro then marched south with a puppet ruler and Inca allies, and on 15 November 1533 entered Cusco, the Inca capital. The Inca Empire had fallen, though resistance continued from Vilcabamba until 1572.

name: Songhai Empire
summary: From Gao, Sonni Ali (r. 1464–1492) turned Songhai into the Sahel's leading power, taking Timbuktu and Djenné and much of Mali's former territory. Askia Muhammad I, who seized power in 1493, reorganised the state, made a celebrated pilgrimage to Mecca and pushed its frontiers further. After his overthrow in 1528 civil wars weakened the empire, and in 1591 a Moroccan army with firearms routed the Songhai at Tondibi and sacked Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné.

events.text: c. 1464: Sonni Ali takes power at Gao
events.detail: Songhai was a kingdom on the middle Niger river, centred on Gao, that had once been subject to the Mali Empire. As Mali weakened in the 15th century, the Sonni dynasty of Gao grew more powerful. Around 1464 Sonni Ali, later called Sonni Ali Ber ('the Great'), came to power. A brilliant general, he built a powerful army and a fleet of boats on the Niger. Over his 28-year reign he turned a small state into an empire, and Songhai appears on the map as the rising power of the Niger Bend.

events.text: Songhai conquers Mema from the Mali Empire
events.detail: Mema was a region west of Timbuktu and one of the oldest provinces of the Mali Empire. In the 1460s Sonni Ali's predecessor, Sulayman Dama, attacked it. According to the Mali Empire article, Songhai completed its conquest in 1465, early in Sonni Ali's reign. The article on Sonni Ali says Songhai already controlled the Niger valley as far as Mema when he came to power. The conquest pushed Songhai's frontier west into Mali's old heartland and marked the shift of power from Mali to Songhai.

events.text: Sonni Ali takes Timbuktu from the Tuareg
events.detail: Timbuktu, the great trading and learning city on the Niger Bend, had been held by Tuareg Berbers since Mali lost it in 1433–1434. Its leaders asked Sonni Ali for help against the Tuareg. He took the city in 1468 (the Sonni Ali article dates the request to 1469). Muslim chroniclers accused him of brutality toward its people and especially its scholars, whom he saw as allies of the Tuareg. Controlling Timbuktu gave Songhai the terminus of the trans-Saharan caravan routes, and with it great wealth.

events.text: Djenné surrenders after a long siege
events.detail: Djenné was a rich trading town in the inland Niger delta, linked by river to Timbuktu, and its people resisted Sonni Ali's attempts to take it. He used his fleet of river boats to lay siege to the town. According to tradition the siege lasted seven years, and in 1473 the starving townspeople finally surrendered (one passage in the Songhai Empire article gives 1475). With Djenné, Songhai controlled the trade of the whole middle Niger, from the gold-producing south to the Saharan routes.

events.text: Sonni Ali dies; his son Sonni Baru succeeds
events.detail: Sonni Ali died on 6 November 1492 in uncertain circumstances (the Tarikh al-Sudan says he drowned while crossing the Niger), and his son Sonni Baru succeeded him. Like his father, who had practised a mixture of Islam and traditional religion, Baru drew his support from the traditional religious leaders of the Songhai. Muslim leaders in the towns distrusted him, and within months one of Sonni Ali's generals used Baru's lack of Islamic faith as the reason for a rebellion.

events.text: Askia Muhammad defeats Sonni Baru at Anfao and takes power
events.detail: Muhammad Ture, one of Sonni Ali's generals, rose up against Sonni Baru in 1492, claiming that he was not a faithful Muslim. In April 1493 he defeated Baru at the Battle of Anfao, outside Gao, and took power with the title Askia. He founded the Askia dynasty and became known as Askia the Great. He reorganised the empire with a strong bureaucracy and a professional army, and he made Islam a pillar of his rule, inviting Muslim scholars to his court. Under him Songhai grew into one of the largest empires in African history.

events.text: Askia Muhammad's pilgrimage to Mecca (dated 1496 or 1497–98)
events.detail: In 1496 Askia Muhammad set out on the pilgrimage to Mecca with 500 horsemen and 1,000 foot soldiers, carrying a great deal of gold (one source dates the journey to 1497–1498). He gave generously to charity, including a hostel in Medina for West African pilgrims, and returned nearly two years later with large debts. The titles of al-hajj and caliph that he brought back strengthened his religious prestige. He returned determined to spread Islam, building schools and mosques and bringing scholars to Timbuktu.

events.text: Songhai defeats a Mali army and seizes Diafunu
events.detail: After his pilgrimage, Askia Muhammad launched a series of campaigns to expand the empire in every direction. To the west, his armies attacked the shrinking Mali Empire. According to the Mali Empire article, in 1502 Songhai forces defeated the Malian general Fati Quali Keita and seized the province of Diafunu, though the article on Askia Muhammad dates its capture to 1501. His campaigns also brought the salt mines of Taghaza in the Sahara within its borders.

events.text: Askia Muhammad deposed by his son Musa
events.detail: By the 1520s Askia Muhammad was well over 70, ill and secretly blind, while his many sons quarrelled. In August 1528 his son Musa forced him to abdicate and took the throne. Musa ruled only three years before his own brothers killed him, and a later ruler exiled the old king to an island in the Niger. The empire entered a period of plots and civil wars, though it kept its territory. Askia Muhammad finally died in 1538.

events.text: Askia Dawud's reign (to 1582) brings stability and victories
events.detail: After years of succession disputes, Askia Dawud, another son of Askia Muhammad, became ruler in 1549 and reigned for 33 years until 1582. His reign brought stability and security, and a string of military successes. He fought the Mossi and Borgu, and in 1550 and 1558 he attacked Mali, whose mansa gave him his daughter in marriage. But his army did not adopt firearms, and it still relied on spears and arrows. Meanwhile Morocco began demanding the revenues of the Taghaza salt mines, a sign of trouble to come.

events.text: Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco sends Judar Pasha across the Sahara
events.detail: Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco wanted control of the trans-Saharan trade and believed, wrongly, that Songhai owned gold mines. When Askia Ishaq II refused his demand for payment for the Taghaza salt, he decided to invade. On 16 October 1590 an army left Marrakesh under Judar Pasha, a commander of Spanish origin, with thousands of soldiers, many armed with arquebuses (early muskets), and a train of 8,000 camels. Estimates of its size vary from 4,000 to 20,000 men. After a hard four-month crossing of the Sahara it reached the Niger in February 1591.

events.text: Moroccan musketeers rout the Songhai at Tondibi; Gao sacked
events.detail: On 13 March 1591 the Moroccan army met the much larger Songhai army of Askia Ishaq II near Tondibi, just north of Gao. The Songhai tried to break the Moroccan lines with a stampede of cattle, but the Moroccans' guns turned the tide, and the Songhai cavalry fled or were cut down. Judar Pasha went on to sack Gao, whose people had already fled, then moved on to Timbuktu and Djenné. The Songhai Empire collapsed. Moroccan soldiers ruled the Niger Bend from Timbuktu, and Songhai disappears from the map.
